modules.summary: Mean and median are not formulas to memorise but behaviours to feel. The mean is a balance point, and both measures respond in predictable ways when data is added, removed, shifted, scaled, or read from a frequency table.

media.title: The Graph That Told Two Stories
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening on honest numbers and wrong impressions, and withholds every method: no summary is defined, no graph is corrected and no rule about axes is stated.
media.description: One line graph shows a company's sales soaring, and the same figures replotted from zero show them barely moving, and both graphs are honest. A class average drops far enough to change how the class is described when one absent student's zero is added in.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse suspicion of single summaries and of graphs, before either is analysed. Key teaching points: 1) A graph's axis choice changes the impression it leaves. 2) One extra value can move a mean noticeably. 3) Colour choices can exaggerate a pattern. 4) Correct numbers can still mislead. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often trust a graph because the underlying data is correct. 2) Students often ignore how a summary was constructed. Pause points: 0:32, at the end of one absent student: ask which sales graph the class believes. 1:15, just before the opening question: ask why one zero moved the class average so much. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what an average is entitled to say. After viewing, ask what they check first on a new graph.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Let correct numbers leave wrong impressions three times over, so the entitlement of a summary becomes the question.

  STORY
    A sales graph, a class average and a rainfall chart are all accurate and all misleading.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the sales graph: one version shows sales soaring and the same figures replotted from zero show them barely moving
    claim about the two: both graphs are honest
    the class: thirty students, with a mean of 62 marks
    what happens: one absent student's zero is added in, and the mean falls to 60
    the consequence: the drop is enough to change how the whole class is described
    the rainfall chart: a clever colour scale makes an average monsoon look like a disaster
    the claim: every number in the clip is correct, and almost every impression it leaves is wrong
    withheld: every method, every correction and every rule about axes

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 90 seconds across 6 scenes.

    Scene 1. Soaring, or barely moving
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 2.8 s  Create(s1_axis) over 0.8 s, to lay the common baseline.
      at 5.3 s  GrowFromEdge(s1_bars) over 1.6 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to grow every bar up from the baseline.
      at 8.6 s  Write(s1_bars) over 1.0 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to put the value and the name on each bar.
      at 11.2 s  FadeIn(s1_barnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 13.7 s  FadeOut(s1_axis, s1_bars, s1_barnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "One line graph shows a company's sales soaring away, and the very same figures replotted with the axis starting from zero show them barely moving at all. Both of those graphs are perfectly honest."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. One absent student
      Duration: 16 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 3.3 s  Create(s2_table) over 1.8 s, lag_ratio 0.22, to reveal the table row by row.
      at 7.2 s  FadeIn(s2_tnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.2 s  Indicate(s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to hold the eye on what has just appeared.
      at 13.2 s  FadeOut(s2_table, s2_tnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Then a class of thirty has its average marks reported, one absent student's zero is added into the pile, and the average drops far enough to change how the whole class gets described."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. A monsoon, recoloured
      Duration: 14 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s2_caption, s3_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.4 s  Create(s3_grid) over 1.6 s, lag_ratio 0.06, to build the array square by square.
      at 5.4 s  FadeIn(s3_shaded) over 1.1 s, lag_ratio 0.12, to fill the cells that are being counted.
      at 7.8 s  Write(s3_glabel) over 0.8 s, to name the array.
      at 9.9 s  FadeIn(s3_gnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.1 s  FadeOut(s3_grid, s3_shaded, s3_glabel, s3_gnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "A rainfall chart with a clever colour scale makes a perfectly average monsoon look like an outright disaster, and nobody changed a single reading anywhere on it to manage that."
      Persists into the next scene: s3_caption.

    Scene 4. Correct, and misleading
      Duration: 14 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s3_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s3_caption, s4_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.5 s  FadeIn(s4_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 4.8 s  Indicate(s4_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 7.0 s  FadeIn(s4_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 9.8 s  FadeIn(s4_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.0 s  FadeOut(s4_sub, s4_lines, s4_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Every single number in this clip is correct, and almost every impression that it leaves behind is wrong, because all the important choices were made long before any reader arrived."
      Persists into the next scene: s4_caption.

    Scene 5. What is it entitled to say?
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s4_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s4_caption, s5_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 3.1 s  FadeIn(s5_chips) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.18, to bring the row in one chip at a time.
      at 6.6 s  Indicate(s5_chips) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.1, to sweep across the whole row.
      at 9.5 s  FadeIn(s5_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 12.4 s  FadeOut(s5_chips, s5_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "So the question is not whether the numbers are right. It is what a single figure, or a single picture, is actually entitled to claim about a whole group of people."
      Persists into the next scene: s5_caption.

    Scene 6. The opening question
      Duration: 15 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s5_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s6_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.9 s  Create(s6_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.4 s  FadeIn(s6_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 8.9 s  Circumscribe(s6_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      at 12.2 s  Indicate(s6_question) over 0.9 s, to hold the eye on what has just appeared.
      Narration: "That is the question this chapter exists to answer, and it turns out to matter far more than any of the arithmetic that goes into producing the figure in the first place."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No rule, formula, method or answer from any later part of the chapter.
    Nothing is taught here; the film only opens questions.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. Nothing in the film teaches a rule or reveals a later result.
    10. The film closes on curiosity about the chapter, not on an answer.

media.title: The mean is a balance point
labels: not halfway between the smallest and largest
media.context: The mean is the balance point, where the total distance to the dots on the left equals the total on the right, not simply halfway between the smallest and largest. The worked example finds the balance point of 4, 8 and 9. The figure balances the beam and measures both sides.
media.description: The mean is a balance point: a labelled figure illustrating the idea, drawn from the worked example 'Find the balance point (mean) of 4, 8, 9'.

media.teaching_notes: Measure the distances either side of a guessed pivot and adjust until they match. Ask whether the balance point has to sit halfway between the extremes. Then add a fourth value and watch the pivot move.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a pivot placed where the distance totals do not match; a dot plotted at the wrong value; a distance bracket that does not match its gap; the midpoint of the extremes presented as the mean; a number line with unequal spacing
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A number line runs across the picture with dots plotted at 4, 8 and 9, drawn as equal weights on a beam. A pivot triangle sits under the line at 7, tinted teal and labelled the balance point. Two distance brackets are drawn: one from 7 back to the dot at 4, labelled 3; and two from 7 out to the dots at 8 and 9, labelled 1 and 2, with a combining strip reading '1 + 2 = 3'. A balance strip reads that the totals match at 3 each, and a working strip reads '4 + 8 + 9 = 21' then '21 divided by 3 = 7'. A crossed out note marks the midpoint of the smallest and largest, at 6.5, as not the mean. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 4; 8; 9; the balance point; 7; 3; 1; 2; 1 + 2 = 3; the totals match; 4 + 8 + 9 = 21; 21 divided by 3 = 7; not halfway between the smallest and largest.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The dots must be plotted at exactly 4, 8 and 9 on an evenly spaced line.
The pivot must sit at 7, with distance totals of 3 on each side.
The working must give 21 divided by 3 equal to 7.
The midpoint of the extremes must be marked as not the mean.
All dots must be drawn as equal weights.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Mean Balance Point
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2, 'Tales by Dots and Lines', the section called The Balancing Act. This is the class's first mechanical meaning for the mean, met before the add-and-divide recipe is leaned on, and it opens the averages thread that the median tool continues. The chapter's own sentence is 'total distance from the mean on the left side = total distance from the mean on the right side', and this tool is that sentence made operable. Nothing later in the chapter is assumed: no deviation, no mean absolute deviation, no weighted mean, no bar notation.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's fulcrum, the true mean and the arrows that explain it.
whatYouLearned: The mean is the balance mark of the data, where the distances on the two sides total the same
Balance is about distances, so the mean is not the crowd and not the middle of the range
Every value pulls on the mean, so moving or adding one value moves it

overview.goal: The student places the fulcrum where a dot plot balances, connects that point to the mean, and explains why the two sides of arrows must total the same.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A long balance beam laid across a working surface, with equal weights hung at the marks of a number line and a sliding wedge underneath it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class splits over whether a beam of weights hangs level under the thickest crowd of them or under a single far one, and the wedge is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A dot plot of equal weights balances exactly at the mean. Distances from the fulcrum are deviations, and at the mean the total pull to the left equals the total pull to the right. This is a property about distances, not about how many points sit on each side.
overview.purpose: The student places the fulcrum where a dot plot balances, connects that point to the mean, and explains why the two sides of arrows must total the same.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Beam fills the main panel with the arrow totals beneath and the value list under those. On a 390 px frame the beam keeps full width and the fulcrum keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the mean while a prediction is still open, and never let the beam look level at a fulcrum that is not the exact mean. A visually level near miss would teach that the mean is approximate.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Each point pulls with a force proportional to its distance from the fulcrum, so the beam is level exactly when the two totals of distances agree. A few far points can outweigh many near ones, which is why the balance point is not where the points are densest and not the midpoint of the range. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

scenes.title: MLa · Easy · Conceptual
scenes.subGoal: The balance point answers to every weight, so it leaves the halfway mark of the range as soon as the weights are unevenly spread.
scenes.animation: Fulcrum drag: the beam angle follows the signed deviation sum continuously, so approaching the mean is felt as the tilt easing.
scenes.explanation: Blackboard lines, in order: The halfway mark of the range listens to the lowest and the highest weight only. | 24 plus 96 is 120. | 120 halved is 60, which is where the student set the fulcrum. | The balance point has to answer to every weight, so total all three. | 96 plus 27 is 123. | 123 plus 24 is 147. | 147 shared equally among three weights is 49. | The fulcrum belongs at 49, so at 60 the beam tips towards the two low weights. Answer: No: it balances at 49, not at the halfway mark 60
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
textAndLabels: A beam carries equal weights at 24, 27 and 96. A student sets the fulcrum halfway between the lowest and the highest weight, at 60. Does the beam balance there?
The data values, always on screen
Both deviation totals, live once the arrows are shown
The mean as an exact fraction, once the prediction is committed

scenes.subGoal: One far weight drags the balance point clear of the crowd, so the fulcrum can rest where there is no data at all.
scenes.animation: Level: at the exact mean the beam settles flat and holds, which marks the balance point as a definite position.
scenes.explanation: Blackboard lines, in order: 27 plus 33 is 60. | 60 plus 28 is 88. | 88 plus 32 is 120. | 120 plus 105 is 225. | 225 shared equally among five weights is 45. | 45 sits beyond the crowd of four and short of the far weight, with nothing on it. Answer: 45, where no weight sits

scenes.title: MLc · Medium · Conceptual
scenes.subGoal: A symmetric set balances at its centre because the arrows cancel in pairs, which is the one case where the halfway mark of the range gives the right answer.
scenes.animation: Point move: the beam re tips immediately, so the dependence on every value is instant rather than recomputed on demand.
scenes.explanation: Blackboard lines, in order: In a symmetric set the outer weights pair up around one centre. | 24 plus 108 is 132. | 132 halved is 66, so that pair has its centre at 66. | 108 minus 66 is 42. | 66 minus 24 is 42. | The two arrows of that pair are equal, so the pair pulls nowhere. | 99 minus 66 is 33. | 66 minus 33 is 33. | The inner pair is equal too, so every arrow cancels and the beam rests at 66. Answer: 66, because every pair of weights sits at equal distances either side of it
scenes.interaction: The agent lands this step with gotoStep, the animation plays, the class predicts out loud, then the agent calls reveal(). The board then fills one line per step.
textAndLabels: The weights 24, 33, 99 and 108 are spread symmetrically. Name the balance point without totalling anything, and say how you know.
The data values, always on screen
Both deviation totals, live once the arrows are shown

learnMode.checkpointPlan: MLa (Easy, Conceptual): The balance point answers to every weight, so it leaves the halfway mark of the range as soon as the weights are unevenly spread. Breaks: Mean confused with the middle of the range. MLb (Medium, Edge Case): One far weight drags the balance point clear of the crowd, so the fulcrum can rest where there is no data at all. Breaks: The balance point assumed to be where most points are, which is the mode. MLc (Medium, Conceptual): A symmetric set balances at its centre because the arrows cancel in pairs, which is the one case where the halfway mark of the range gives the right answer. Breaks: Mean confused with the middle of the range, a rule that agrees only on symmetric data. MLd (Hard, Edge Case): The balance point is a position on the beam, so it need not be whole and need not carry a weight. Breaks: A balance point rejected unless it lands on a weight or on a whole mark. MLe (Hard, Conceptual): Balance is settled by distance from the fulcrum, not by how many weights sit on each side. Breaks: Assuming the fulcrum splits the weights into equal numbers, or rests where most of them are.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the tipped beam with the weights hung at their own marks, the wedge off to one side and the mean hidden, and ask the class to say out loud which mark the beam will hang level at. Commit the class mark on the prediction pad. Targets the opening set of weights with the wedge left of all of them. Never show the mean and never draw the arrows at this call. Call 2. Slide the wedge to the mean so the beam settles flat, then draw the deviation arrows and point at the left total and at the right total in turn. Targets the wedge at the mean of the opening values with the arrows on. Read the mean and both totals from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Move the weight furthest from the wedge one step further out and let the beam re tip while the wedge stays where it is. Targets that one weight moved outward with the wedge unchanged. Name which total grew and read both totals from getState().truth.

hunts: BARE FULCRUM HUNT: build a set whose balance point has no weight on it, then say what pushed it there.
CROWD TEST: build a set where the crowd of weights is nowhere near the fulcrum, and say why the crowd loses.
HALF MARK HUNT: find three sets whose balance point is not a whole mark, and one where it is.
PAIR IT OFF: build a symmetric set, name its balance point before totalling, then check by totalling.
ONE AGAINST MANY: hold two weights still and find where a single weight balances both.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A crowd is a count of weights, and the tip is decided by distance, so a lone far weight can outpull several near ones
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The beam is still tipped when the wedge sits under the thickest crowd of weights
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The balance mark is the mean, never the crowd, and the crowd is the mode

observationsAndConclusions.why: The middle of the range is built from the smallest and the largest value alone and ignores everything between them
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The wedge parked at the middle of the range leaves a lopsided set tipped
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The mean uses every value, so it agrees with the middle of the range only when the set happens to be symmetric

observationsAndConclusions.why: That weight's distance to the wedge changed, so the two totals of distances no longer agree
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Sliding one weight by a single mark re tips the beam at once
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Every value has a say in the mean, which is why the mean shifts whenever any one value moves

media.description: A beam lies across a working surface with equal weights hung at the marks of a number line and a wedge sliding underneath it. The wedge sets the beam's angle from the true signed total, so the tilt eases as the balance mark is approached and the beam settles flat at exactly one place; a quarter-mark miss still tips, because levelness is decided by exact rational arithmetic and never by how the drawing looks. Turning the distance arrows on draws one arrow from every weight to the wedge, labels each with its own distance, and lays the two totals out as two bars sharing one origin and one unit, so the flat beam and the numerical equality are the same fact told twice. Both totals are drawn and printed POSITIVE, because 'how far away?' cannot answer with a negative number, and the signed sum stays inside the tool driving the tilt. A second, clearly labelled tick carries the mark the misconception proposes - the halfway mark of the range - and the level beam is visibly not over it. Dragging a weight re-tips the beam in the same frame, and a single far weight visibly out-pulls a crowd of near ones. Concept teaches the idea in three beats, Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints with the answer already on screen, Practice serves six of thirty reviewed questions on a difficulty ladder with the beam HELD on props until the attempt is in, and Free Play unlocks the wedge, the weights and the arrows with nothing scored.

Beat 3 moves one data point and the beam re tips immediately, so the balance is seen to depend on every value. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setFulcrum, movePoint, showArrows and say. No drag: the agent sets the fulcrum by value.
modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the dot plot from its own values, shows the question, then reveals the balance point, the arrows and the mean together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
modes.normal: Free Play, student operated. The student drags the fulcrum and any point, adds or removes points, and shows the deviation arrows. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.
modes.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own plot. Find the balance point, give the mean, or explain the deviation argument. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's fulcrum, the true mean and the arrows.

theme.premise: A class splits over whether a beam of weights hangs level under the thickest crowd of them or under a single far one, and the wedge is asked to settle it
theme.setting: A long balance beam laid across a working surface, with equal weights hung at the marks of a number line and a sliding wedge underneath it
theme.visualStyle: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration
theme.studentPalette: The warmer accent of the same family, with the score and the Finish button carrying it
theme.teacherPalette: The cool indigo accent, low chrome, high contrast, so a projected board stays readable

practice.rating: all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1, never 0
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's fulcrum, the true mean and the arrows that explain it.

whatYouLearned: The mean is the balance mark of the data, where the distances on the two sides total the same
Balance is about distances, so the mean is not the crowd and not the middle of the range
Every value pulls on the mean, so moving or adding one value moves it

The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: A deviation is the signed distance from a value to the fulcrum. The mean is the point where the deviations either side total the same.
concept.statement: A dot plot of equal weights balances exactly at the mean. Distances from the fulcrum are deviations, and at the mean the total pull to the left equals the total pull to the right. This is a property about distances, not about how many points sit on each side.
misconceptions: Mean confused with the middle of the range.
The balance point assumed to be where most points are, which is the mode.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each point pulls with a force proportional to its distance from the fulcrum, so the beam is level exactly when the two totals of distances agree. A few far points can outweigh many near ones, which is why the balance point is not where the points are densest and not the midpoint of the range.
worked_numbers: Values 2, 3 and 10 balance at 5, since 3 and 2 to the left total 5 and 5 to the right totals 5.
The midpoint of the range would be 6, which is not the balance point.
The mode may be at 2 and the beam still tips.

setWedgeOutcomes.atTheMean: the beam settles flat and holds, and the two totals of distances print as equal
setWedgeOutcomes.aboveTheMean: the beam tips to the left, by the same argument the other way round
setWedgeOutcomes.belowTheMean: the beam tips to the right, because the total of the distances on the right is the larger
setWedgeOutcomes.atTheMiddleOfTheRange: the beam stays tipped for any set that is not symmetric, since only the two extreme values decided that mark
setWedgeOutcomes.underTheThickestCrowd: the beam stays tipped unless the crowd happens to sit at the mean, which is the mode misconception refused in a picture

movePointOutcomes.acrossTheWedge: the weight changes side, so its distance leaves one total and joins the other
movePointOutcomes.towardsTheWedge: that weight's distance shrinks, its side's total falls, and the beam tips the other way
movePointOutcomes.awayFromTheWedge: that weight's distance grows, its side's total rises, and the beam tips further that way

showArrowsOutcomes.on: one signed arrow is drawn from every weight to the wedge and both totals print beneath the beam
showArrowsOutcomes.off: the arrows and both totals clear, leaving the beam and the values only

answer_key.worked: Values 2, 3 and 10 balance at 5, which is the mean, because the deviations total the same on both sides.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn plot: the mean as an exact fraction and the two deviation sums.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational arithmetic, so the level condition is unambiguous. The beam angle is proportional to the signed deviation sum and clamped for display only.
answer_key.ground_truth: mean(values) = the exact rational average. deviations(values, fulcrum) = the signed distances. isLevel(fulcrum) = the two sums agree exactly.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A fulcrum very close to the mean
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The beam is not level, since levelness is decided by exact arithmetic rather than by how the tilt looks.
The beam balances at that point, which the tool states rather than treating as a degenerate case.
The balance point moves well away from the densest cluster, which the tool notes, since that is the mode misconception being addressed.

HALF MARK HUNT: find three sets whose balance point is not a whole mark, and one where it is.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the idea, shown rather than asserted. The beam is level, the wedge sits at 5, and the two totals both read 5 - three and two on the left against one five on the right. Say the chapter's own sentence over it: the total distance to the weights on the left equals the total distance to the weights on the right. Ask the class OUT LOUD, before the beat lands, where they think three weights at 2, 3 and 10 will hang level; the guess is worth more than the answer here because most of a Class 8 room says 6.

Beat 2 is why it works, and it is the misconception refused in a picture rather than in a caption. The same three weights are shown with the wedge parked at 6, the mark halfway between the lowest and the highest, and the beam TIPS: four and three against four, seven against four. Point at the two total bars, not at the beam. The halfway mark listens to only the smallest and the largest value; the balance mark answers to every weight, which is exactly why the two marks part company as soon as the weights are unevenly spread.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its useful edge. One weight moves from 10 out to 13 and the beam re-tips in the same frame with the wedge untouched, so the balance mark has moved from 5 to 6 while two of the three weights never moved at all. Say that every single value has a vote, which is why the mean shifts whenever any one of them does - and that this is the same mechanism that lets one far weight outweigh a crowd of near ones.

media.title: The see-saw that never lies
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the mean as a balance point. Students have no definition. The film must not compute the balance point and must not name the mean.
media.description: A see saw wobbles under uneven weights and then settles at one exact spot. The clip asks where that balancing spot sits, and whether it is simply halfway between the lightest and the heaviest child.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Understand the mean as the balance point of a data set. Key teaching points: 1) Every value pulls on the balance point. 2) A value far from the centre pulls harder. 3) The balance point is not generally halfway between the extremes. 4) It is the total shared equally among the values. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often take the midpoint of the range as the centre. 2) Students often think the centre must be one of the values. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of halfway, surely: ask where the class thinks it balances. 0:23, just before the open question: ask whether halfway is a fair guess. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what makes a see saw balance. After viewing, ask which values pull hardest.

topics.summary: The mean is the balance point of the data, the place where total distance on the left equals total distance on the right, and there is exactly one such point.

content.text:
The mean of some data is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values in the data. The mean is also called the average, or the arithmetic mean; all three names refer to the same number.

The median is the middle value when the data is sorted. Sorting first is part of the definition, since the middle entry of an unsorted list means nothing.

The arithmetic mean is a measure of central tendency, which means it represents the centre of the data. For two numbers, the mean sits exactly halfway between them, so the mean of 3 and 7 is 5 and the mean of 8 and 9 is 8.5.

The mean of some data is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values in the data. The mean is also called the average, or the arithmetic mean; all three names refer to the same number.

The median is the middle value when the data is sorted. Sorting first is part of the definition, since the middle entry of an unsorted list means nothing.

The arithmetic mean is a measure of central tendency, which means it represents the centre of the data. For two numbers, the mean sits exactly halfway between them, so the mean of 3 and 7 is 5 and the mean of 8 and 9 is 8.5.

concepts.concept_name: Mean, median and central tendency - the definition

content.text: The mean is often called the centre of the data, but the centre is not simply halfway between the smallest and largest values. Picture the values as dots on a number line. The mean is the one point where the total of the distances to the dots on its left is exactly equal to the total of the distances to the dots on its right, like the balance point of a see-saw. For 6, 6, 7 and 13 the mean is (6 + 6 + 7 + 13) / 4 = 8. Below 8 the distances add to 2 + 2 + 1 = 5, and above 8 the single distance is 13 - 8 = 5, so the beam balances at 8. There is only one such point, because sliding the marker either way makes one side heavier.

content.text: The mean is often called the centre of the data, but the centre is not simply halfway between the smallest and largest values. Picture the values as dots on a number line. The mean is the one point where the total of the distances to the dots on its left is exactly equal to the total of the distances to the dots on its right, like the balance point of a see-saw. For 6, 6, 7 and 13 the mean is (6 + 6 + 7 + 13) / 4 = 8. Below 8 the distances add to 2 + 2 + 1 = 5, and above 8 the single distance is 13 - 8 = 5, so the beam balances at 8. There is only one such point, because sliding the marker either way makes one side heavier.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that the mean is the sum of the values divided by number of values, also called the average or arithmetic mean, that the median is the middle value of the sorted data, and that the mean is a measure of central tendency. They will compute both for a given set of values.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what makes a point the true centre of a data set through observation and reasoning, and determine that the mean is the single place where the total distance to the values below it equals the total distance to the values above it, not the midpoint of the smallest and largest. They will explain that this balance point is unique, since sliding it either way makes one side heavier than the other.

segments.summary: Mean and median are not formulas to memorise but behaviours to feel. The mean is a balance point, and both measures respond in predictable ways when data is added, removed, shifted, scaled, or read from a frequency table.

media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A number line carries dots at 4, 8, 9 and 11 with a pivot at 8 labelled the old mean. A new dot at 16 is dropped in, tinted amber, with an arrow showing it landing well to the right of the pivot and a tag reading above the mean. The pivot then slides right along the line to 9.6, drawn in its new position and labelled the new mean, with a working strip reading '32 + 16 = 48' then '48 divided by 5 = 9.6'. A rule strip beneath gives the three cases: a value above the mean pulls it up, one below pulls it down, and one exactly equal leaves it still, each with a small arrow diagram. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: 4; 8; 9; 11; the old mean: 8; 16; above the mean; the new mean: 9.6; 32 + 16 = 48; 48 divided by 5 = 9.6; above pulls up, below pulls down, equal leaves it still.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The original set must be 4, 8, 9 and 11 with a mean of 8.
The new value 16 must sit above the mean and the new mean must be 9.6.
The working must read 32 plus 16 equals 48, divided by 5.
The pivot must slide toward the new value.
All three rule cases must be stated correctly.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Mean Fair Share
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2, 'Tales by Dots and Lines' — the mean read as a FAIR SHARE, beside the balance-point reading. The class has met 'average', 'mean', 'observations', 'median' and 'dot plot' from Class 7; it has NOT met x-bar, sigma, 'measure of central tendency' or 'deviation', and none of those appear anywhere in this tool. The formula is written as the book writes it: Mean = total ÷ number of values. A fractional level is written as a MIXED NUMBER (45 and a half), with a decimal only ever beside it.

overview.goal: The student levels a set of bars to equal height, identifies that height as the mean, and says what a fractional mean means for whole objects.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A row of stacked unit blocks standing on one baseline, the way counters are stacked in columns on a desk and then evened out by hand. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is asked what height a row of uneven stacks will reach when they are evened out, and whether the answer can be a height no stack ever stood at.
overview.concept: Levelling a set of bars without changing the total gives the mean. Because the total is fixed and the bars must end equal, the level is forced rather than chosen, which is what makes the mean the unique fair share. When the total does not divide evenly the level is a fraction, and that is a real answer rather than an impossibility.
overview.purpose: The student levels a set of bars to equal height, identifies that height as the mean, and says what a fractional mean means for whole objects.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Bars fill the main panel with the total above and the mean readout beneath. On a 390 px frame the bars narrow but every unit stays at least 12 px tall. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not draw the level line while a prediction is still open, and never round a fractional level to a whole unit. A rounded level would deny the answer the second stage exists to produce.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Moving a unit from one bar to another leaves the total untouched, so any levelling reaches the same height: the total divided by the number of bars. That is why the level cannot be argued about. If the division leaves a remainder the level lies between whole values, which is exactly what a fractional mean is. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: MLa (Easy, Conceptual): The level a set of bars settles at is a height they share out, so it need not match any bar that was there before. Breaks: Mean assumed to be a data value. MLb (Medium, Edge Case): An empty bar still counts in the sharing, because it is one of the things the total is being spread across. Breaks: Dropping an empty bar from the count, which lifts the level. MLc (Medium, Edge Case): A level of half a block is a real answer about the sharing, not a sign that the sharing failed. Breaks: A fractional mean rejected as impossible because the data are whole objects. MLd (Hard, Edge Case): The level depends on how many bars share the total, so bringing in a bar changes it with no change to the blocks at all. Breaks: Believing the level can only change when blocks are added or removed. MLe (Hard, Conceptual): The level answers to the total and the number of bars alone, so rearranging blocks between bars leaves it exactly where it was. Breaks: Believing every change to the bars must change the mean.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with uneven bars and the level HIDDEN, and asks what height they will all reach. Beat 2 moves units from tall to short with the total unchanged until every bar is equal, and the level is announced as the mean. Beat 3 adds a bar so the total no longer levels exactly, and the bars settle at a fractional height. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with moveUnit, autoLevel, addBar and say. No drag: the agent moves units by count.
whatYouLearned: Evening out a set of stacks without changing the total lands them all at the mean
The mean is the total divided by the number of values, and it can be a fraction even when every value is whole
A value of zero still counts as a value, so it lowers the mean
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the uneven stacks with the running total shown and no level line drawn, and ask the class to say out loud what height every stack will reach once they are evened out. Commit the class height on the prediction pad. Targets the opening stacks with the total on. Never draw the level line at this call. Call 2. Move units from the tallest stack to the shortest one at a time, pointing at the total readout each time it fails to move, until the row is level and the line is drawn. Targets the opening stacks levelled with the total on. Read the level from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Add one more stack so that the total no longer divides evenly, and let the row settle at a height that runs through a cut block. Targets the row with the extra stack and the level line on. Say what the fraction means for whole objects and read the level from getState().truth.

hunts: NOBODY IS THERE: build a row whose level matches none of its bars, then one where it matches exactly one.
HALF A BLOCK: find three rows whose level lands midway up a block, and say what the fraction means.
EMPTY BAR: level a row, add an empty bar, and say how far the level fell before you check.
MOVE A BLOCK: carry blocks around without changing the level, and say what you are keeping fixed.
ONE BAR ONLY: level a row of a single bar and say why the level and the bar agree there.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A move takes from one stack exactly what it gives to another, so the total is untouched and the level is the total over the number of stacks
observationsAndConclusions.observe: However the units are moved, the stacks always finish at the same height
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The mean is forced by the total and the count, which is why it cannot be argued about

observationsAndConclusions.why: The level is the total shared out, and sharing does not stop being possible because the answer is not whole
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A total that does not divide evenly leaves the top block cut, and the level line runs through it
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A fractional mean is an answer about the sharing, not a claim that a fraction of an object exists

observationsAndConclusions.why: The same total is now shared between more stacks, so each stack's share is smaller
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Adding an empty stack drops the level even though nothing was taken away
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The mean depends on the count as well as the total, so a value of zero is a value and not an absence

media.description: A row of unit-block stacks stands on one baseline with the running total printed above it. Blocks are carried from a tall stack to a short one and the total readout refuses to move, so the height the row finally reaches is forced rather than chosen: it is the total shared equally between the stacks, which is the mean. The level is drawn as a dashed line across the whole row and is never rounded — when the total does not divide evenly the line runs through the middle of a block, and that block is drawn cut, filled to its true fraction, with the level printed as a mixed number. Because the dashed line is placed by the same function that prints the readout and grades the answer, the picture and the number can never disagree. Concept runs three beats: level a row, then rearrange the same twelve blocks so the level does not move and no bar stands on it, then bring in a fourth bar so the level falls and lands mid-block. Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints, each drawn from its own numbers and opening with its answer already on screen. Practice serves six of thirty reviewed items on a difficulty ladder, each rendering the bars its own question names, with the level withheld until the student has committed an answer. Free Play unlocks the drag, the auto level, the bar count and the total readout with nothing scored.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the data from its own values, shows the question, then reveals the levelling, the total and the mean together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with uneven bars and the level HIDDEN, and asks what height they will all reach. Beat 2 moves units from tall to short with the total unchanged until every bar is equal, and the level is announced as the mean. Beat 3 adds a bar so the total no longer levels exactly, and the bars settle at a fractional height. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with moveUnit, autoLevel, addBar and say. No drag: the agent moves units by count.

Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the levelled bars.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student drags units between bars, auto levels, adds or removes bars, and shows the running total. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: The mean is the level all the bars reach when the total is shared equally. It may be a fraction even when every bar started whole.
concept.statement: Levelling a set of bars without changing the total gives the mean. Because the total is fixed and the bars must end equal, the level is forced rather than chosen, which is what makes the mean the unique fair share. When the total does not divide evenly the level is a fraction, and that is a real answer rather than an impossibility.
prerequisites: fractions as parts of a whole
misconceptions: Mean assumed to be a data value.
A fractional mean rejected as impossible because the data are whole objects.
concept.why_it_is_true: Moving a unit from one bar to another leaves the total untouched, so any levelling reaches the same height: the total divided by the number of bars. That is why the level cannot be argued about. If the division leaves a remainder the level lies between whole values, which is exactly what a fractional mean is.
worked_numbers: Bars of 2, 4 and 6 level at 4, which is the mean.
Bars of 2, 3 and 6 total 11 and level at 11 over 3.
Adding a bar of 0 changes the level even though the total does not.

extra: Sweets shared equally among the children at a table, with the last child holding a fraction of one
Money pooled for a gift and split evenly between the givers
Water poured between glasses of the same width until every level matches
Bricks moved along a row of stacks until every stack stands the same height
Chairs moved between rooms until each room holds the same number
The pages of a book divided evenly over the days left before it must go back
A week's earnings shared equally over the seven days to give a daily figure
Seeds dealt equally into trays, where the leftover seeds make the share fractional
Overs shared equally between the bowlers of a side, where the share is not a whole over
Rice divided evenly into bags of equal size, with a scoop left over that has to be split
textbook: The fair share reading of the average from the earlier class, used to explain why including a value equal to the average changes nothing
A collection in which every value is raised by the same fixed amount, and the average seen to rise by exactly that amount
A collection in which every value is multiplied by the same fixed number, and the average multiplied by it too
Heights measured with shoes on, corrected by taking the added thickness off the average itself instead of measuring every student again
The average of a long run of consecutive natural numbers, found without adding them one at a time
The average of a long run of odd numbers, and of a long run of multiples of one number, read off the same way
A frequency table where each value carries how many times it occurs, shared out into a single level height

placement.where: The second meaning for the mean, beside the balance point. Levelling is what makes adding or removing a value visibly move it.

addBarOutcomes.aStackOfZero: the total holds and the count rises, so the level falls
addBarOutcomes.aStackAtTheLevel: the level does not move at all, since the new stack brings exactly its own share
addBarOutcomes.aStackAboveTheLevel: the level rises, because the new stack brings more than a fair share
addBarOutcomes.aStackBelowTheLevel: the level falls, because the new stack brings less than a fair share

moveUnitOutcomes.shortToTall: the row gets less level, and the total readout still does not move
moveUnitOutcomes.tallToShort: the two stacks come closer to level and the total readout does not move
moveUnitOutcomes.betweenTwoEqualStacks: two equal stacks become uneven again, which shows that levelness is not preserved by moving but the total is

autoLevelOutcomes.on: units redistribute one at a time until every stack reaches the same height and the level line is drawn
autoLevelOutcomes.off: the row is left exactly as the student built it and the level line clears

showTotalOutcomes.on: the running total prints above the row and can be watched holding still under every move
showTotalOutcomes.off: the total is hidden, so only the shape of the row is on screen

answer_key.worked: Bars of 2, 4 and 6 level at 4, because the total 12 shared between 3 bars gives 4.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn bars: the total, the mean as an exact fraction, and the levelled height.
answer_key.precision: Exact rational mean. Fractional heights are rendered honestly rather than rounded to whole units.
answer_key.ground_truth: total(bars) = the exact sum, invariant under unit moves. mean(bars) = total over the bar count, as an exact fraction. levelledHeight = the mean.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A total that does not divide evenly
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The bars settle at a fractional height drawn honestly, and the tool asks what that means when the data are whole objects.
The total is unchanged but the mean falls, which the tool states, since dividing the same total among more bars lowers the share.
Allowed and counted, since an absent value is not the same as a bar that is not there.
The total readout does not move at all, which is held on screen so the invariance is the visible fact.
Already level, and its height is the mean, which the tool says rather than treating as trivial.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example adding a bar a child names and showing the level fall.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

tool_config.tool_objective: The student levels a set of bars to equal height, identifies that height as the mean, and says what a fractional mean means for whole objects.

steps: 24 plus 63 is 87.
87 plus 81 is 168.
168 shared equally among three bars is 56.
Every bar now stands at 56.
None of the three bars started there, and none had to.
items.answer: 56 blocks each, and no bar was already at that height
items.method: Level a set of bars and check the level against the bars themselves
items.question: Three bars hold 24, 63 and 81 blocks. Levelled to the same height, how many blocks does each bar hold, and which bar was already at that height?

stickers.type_method: Level a set of bars and check the level against the bars themselves

items.checkpoint: The level a set of bars settles at is a height they share out, so it need not match any bar that was there before.
items.misconception: Mean assumed to be a data value.

steps: 24 plus 57 is 81.
81 plus 27 is 108.
Sharing 108 among the three bars that have blocks would give 36 each.
But the empty bar is standing on the baseline too, so it is one of the sharers.
108 shared equally among four bars is 27.
The empty bar ends up holding 27, taken from the others.
items.answer: 27 blocks each, not 36
items.method: Level a set that includes a bar holding nothing

visual_behaviour.never: Do not draw the level line while a prediction is still open, and never round a fractional level to a whole unit. A rounded level would deny the answer the second stage exists to produce.
visual_behaviour.scene: Vertical bars built from unit blocks on a common baseline, with a dashed level line drawn once the bars are equal. The running total sits above. A fractional level is drawn as a partial block rather than snapped.
visual_behaviour.layout: Bars fill the main panel with the total above and the mean readout beneath. On a 390 px frame the bars narrow but every unit stays at least 12 px tall.
readouts: The running total, always on screen and unchanging under moves
The mean as an exact fraction, once predicted
animations: Unit move: a block travels from one bar to another and the total readout pulses without changing, which is the invariant made watchable.
Level: bars converge to a common height and the dashed line is drawn last, so the level is reached rather than assumed.
Fractional settle: the final partial block is drawn at its true height, so a fractional mean is seen honestly.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Bar width is derived from the panel and the bar count so every unit block stays at least 12 px tall; the bars narrow rather than the blocks shrinking below that.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The blocks have to be moved and the total watched holding still before the total over the count is written, or the division is a procedure and the fractional answer looks like a mistake in it

mathematical_facts: Moving a unit from one stack to another leaves the total untouched, so every way of evening out ends at the same height
That height is the total divided by the number of stacks, which is the mean
When the total does not divide evenly the level sits between two whole marks, and a fractional mean is a real answer
Adding a stack of zero raises the number of stacks without raising the total, so the level falls

teaching_notes: Beat 1 levels 2, 4 and 6 to 4 — and 4 is one of the bars, which is exactly the trap. Say the level out loud and let the class notice it matched a bar, because beat 2 is about to take that away.

Beat 2 is the whole argument. The same twelve blocks are rearranged to 1, 3 and 8: the total readout does not move, the dashed line does not move, and now NO bar stands on it. The picture, not a caption, refutes 'the level must be one of the bar heights'.

Beat 3 brings in a fourth bar of 3 — below the level — so the level falls to three and three quarters and the line runs through the middle of a block. Read the mixed number off the screen and say what the quarter means for whole blocks; never round it.

media.context: The mean holds still when the added values balance across it. The worked example has the set 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 with mean 10 and adds the pair 4 and 16. The figure shows the two new weights pulling equally and the pivot staying put.

media.title: One new player changes everything
media.context: This hook opens the topic on moving and unchanging means. Students know the balance point. The film must not say which way the mean moves and must not give the value that leaves it unchanged.
media.description: A team's average score is shown, and then a single new player walks on and the average visibly slides. Which way did it move, and could a newcomer ever join and leave the average exactly where it was?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Predict how the mean moves when a value is added or removed. Key teaching points: 1) A new value below the mean pulls it down. 2) A new value above the mean pulls it up. 3) A new value equal to the mean leaves it unchanged. 4) The size of the move depends on how far the value is and how many there are. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often recompute from scratch instead of reasoning about the pull. 2) Students often think any new value must change the mean. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of could it stay put?: ask which way the mean will move before it is shown. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what score would leave it alone. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what the new mean is. After viewing, ask how far a value has to be to matter.

topics.summary: Adding a value above the mean raises it, below lowers it, equal leaves it; removing reverses this. The mean holds still exactly when the changed values balance across it.

content.text: When you drop a new value into a data set, the balance point slides. If the new value is above the current mean it pulls the mean up; if it is below, it pulls the mean down; and if it is exactly equal to the mean, the mean does not move at all. Removing a value works in reverse. Take away a value that was above the mean and the mean drops, because the thing holding the balance up is gone; take away a value below the mean and the mean rises. So the direction never depends on whether you added or removed. It depends only on where the value sits compared with the current mean.

content.text: You might think any change to the data must change the mean, but it need not. The mean holds still whenever the values you add balance across it, pulling down as much as they pull up. The simplest case is a pair that is equally far from the mean on each side, like 4 and 16 around a mean of 10. More generally, the mean stays fixed exactly when the inserted values have the same mean as the data, because then they are just extra fair shares. Two values below can be balanced by one value far enough above, as long as the total distance below equals the total distance above. Removing a balanced group works the same way. But values all on one side, say two values both below the mean, must move it.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what happens to the balance point when a value joins or leaves a data set through observation and reasoning, and determine that a value above the current mean pulls it up, a value below pulls it down, and a value equal to it leaves it fixed, with removing a value doing the reverse. They will explain that the direction depends only on where the value sits relative to the mean, not on the act of adding or removing.

segments.summary: Mean and median are not formulas to memorise but behaviours to feel. The mean is a balance point, and both measures respond in predictable ways when data is added, removed, shifted, scaled, or read from a frequency table.

topics.summary: Adding a fixed number to every value shifts the mean by that number; multiplying every value by a number scales the mean by that number. Both are exact shortcuts, not estimates.

content.text: Suppose you add the same number to every value in a collection. The whole dot plot slides along the number line without changing shape, and the mean slides with it by the same amount. Add 10 to every value and the mean goes up by 10; subtract 3 from every value and the mean goes down by 3. You do not need to re-add all the numbers. Why does it work? If there are n values and you add c to each, the total goes up by n times c, but the count is still n, so dividing gives an extra c. For example, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 has mean 30, and adding 5 to each gives a mean of 35.

content.text: Now suppose you multiply every value in a collection by the same number instead of adding. The dot plot stretches away from zero, the spread grows, and the mean scales by that same number. Double every value and the mean doubles; multiply every value by 3 and the mean triples; take half of every value and the mean halves. Why? The total is just the values added together, so multiplying each value by a number multiplies the whole total by that number. The count of values does not change, so dividing the bigger total by the same count gives a mean scaled by the same factor. For example, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 has mean 30, and doubling every value gives a mean of 60.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what adding the same number to every value does to the centre through observation and reasoning, and determine that adding a fixed number to each value raises the mean by that number and subtracting a fixed number lowers it by that number, with no need to add the whole set again. They will explain that the total grows by the count times the added number while the count itself stays the same, so the mean shifts by exactly that number.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what multiplying every value by the same number does to the centre through observation and reasoning, and determine that multiplying each value by a number multiplies the mean by that same number, so doubling every value doubles the mean and halving every value halves it. They will explain that scaling each value scales the whole total while the count of values stays the same, so the mean scales by exactly that factor.

segments.summary: Mean and median are not formulas to memorise but behaviours to feel. The mean is a balance point, and both measures respond in predictable ways when data is added, removed, shifted, scaled, or read from a frequency table.

media.title: Median Finder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Part 2, 'Tales by Dots and Lines' — the median of ungrouped data, read by POSITION on the ordered list. Odd count: the ((n + 1) ÷ 2)th term. Even count: the average of the (n ÷ 2)th and the (n ÷ 2 + 1)th terms, which is why the tool NAMES BOTH middle positions rather than printing a '2.5th place'. The mean is taught as the balance point elsewhere in this chapter, so every word here is positional — 'count in from both ends' — and never 'balancing'. Quartile, percentile, cumulative frequency, distribution, central tendency and outlier are not used: the class has not met them.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. whatYouLearned: The median is the value at the middle position of the sorted data, so sorting comes first
For a count of n the middle position is the n plus 1 over 2 th one
With an even count the median is the midpoint of the two middle values, which need not be a value in the data

overview.goal: The student orders a data set, identifies the median for both odd and even counts, and states the position rule for any count n.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A strip of numbered cards laid left to right on a working surface, with a pointer that can be pushed along underneath it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is asked which card will end up in the middle before the cards have been put in order, and what to do when no card is in the middle at all.
overview.concept: The median is found by position, not by value, so the data must be sorted first. For an odd count one card sits in the middle. For an even count no card does, and the midpoint of the two middle values is used, which is a decision rather than something read off the strip.
overview.purpose: The student orders a data set, identifies the median for both odd and even counts, and states the position rule for any count n.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Strip fills the main panel with the marker beneath and the median readout under that. On a 390 px frame the strip scrolls horizontally and every card keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not allow the marker on an unsorted strip, and do not round an even count median. Allowing either would teach that the median can be read without ordering or that it must be a data value.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Sorting puts the values in order of size, so the middle position is the value with as many below as above. Without sorting the middle position means nothing. When the count is even there are two such candidates and no card between them, so a convention is needed, and the midpoint is the one that keeps the same number of values on each side. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: MLa (Easy, Edge Case): The median is the middle of the ordered strip, so ordering is not tidying up, it is the step that creates the middle. Breaks: Median taken from the unsorted list. MLb (Medium, Edge Case): An even count has no middle card, so the median is the point halfway between the middle two and need not be a value in the data. Breaks: Believing the median must be one of the cards. MLc (Medium, Edge Case): The middle position is counted over cards, not over the different values, so a repeat holds its place in the queue. Breaks: Removing repeats before counting to the middle. MLd (Hard, Edge Case): The median is a position on the ordered strip, so it can fall between two cards and need not be a value anybody recorded. Breaks: Believing the median must be one of the data values. MLe (Hard, Conceptual): The median position is fixed by how many cards there are, so it can be named before any value is known. Breaks: The middle position confused with the middle value of the range.
