conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the jumbled strip with the pointer locked, and ask the class to say out loud which value will end up in the middle once the cards are in order. Commit the class value on the prediction pad. Targets the opening jumbled cards with the pointer locked. Never sort the strip at this call. Call 2. Sort the cards into increasing order, point at the sorted badge, and let the pointer unlock and settle under the middle card. Targets the opening cards sorted ascending. Read the median and the middle position from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Add one card so the count turns even and the pointer lands under a gap with no card above it. Targets the sorted strip with one card added. State the rule the class must agree on for the gap, and read the resulting median from getState().truth.

hunts: SHUFFLE TEST: deal a strip, read the median, shuffle it and read again, and say why nothing moved.
GAP HUNT: build strips whose median sits in a gap, and say what the count has in common.
REPEAT RUN: fill a strip with repeats until the median stops moving, and say what stopped it.
NAME IT FIRST: set a count, name the middle position before dealing, then deal and check.
ONE CARD: put a single card on the strip and say why it is its own median.

observationsAndConclusions.why: A middle position is only a middle when the values run in order of size, so before sorting there is nothing for the pointer to mark
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The pointer will not move under a jumbled strip at all
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Sorting is not tidying up before the real work; it is the work that makes the position mean something

observationsAndConclusions.why: Reversing the order leaves the middle position where it was, since it is the same number of cards from either end
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Sorting the same cards from largest to smallest leaves the pointer under the same card
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The median is fixed by the data and not by which way round it is written out

observationsAndConclusions.why: An even count has two cards with an equal number below and above, so no single card holds the middle
observationsAndConclusions.observe: With an even count the pointer sits under a gap and no card is under it
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The midpoint of the two middle values is a convention chosen to keep the count on each side equal, and it may be a value no card carries

media.description: A strip of numbered cards laid left to right on a plain working plate, with a triangular pointer beneath it. The pointer REFUSES to seat while the strip is jumbled — it wobbles and stays dashed — so ordering is not tidying up before the real work, it is the work that gives a middle position its meaning. Once the cards are in order the position numbers 1, 2, 3 … appear under them and the pointer locks on the ((n + 1) ÷ 2)th place, drawn from ONE division of the strip's width so all n places are identical to the pixel; a bracket over each side prints how many cards are below and above, and the two counts are equal. On an odd count the pointer lands under a single card. On an even count it lands under the GAP between two, where the median pill turns dashed to say out loud that no card sits there, and the value prints as an exact decimal — 53.5, never 53½, never a vulgar fraction and never rounded to 54. Sorting the same cards from high to low is accepted and leaves the answer untouched, because the middle place is the same distance from either end. Adding or removing a card steps the pointer along the places, so the position rule for a count of n is something the class watches rather than recites. Where a worked example strikes out repeats, the struck strip is drawn BESIDE the full one with its own pointer, so five cards and three cards visibly disagree; where a question is about the midpoint of the range, that marker is drawn too, with the 4-below / 1-above count that refutes it; and a strip of 65 face-down cards is drawn as the schematic it must be, with the 33rd place named before a single card is turned over.

scenes.subGoal: Explore the picture with nothing scored and nothing required
scenes.onScreen: The strip, the cards, the marker, every control, no score and no question. Jumbled cards with the marker locked and every card draggable.
scenes.animation: Card move: the card slides to its new slot and the others shuffle, so ordering is a rearrangement rather than a relabelling.
scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.
scenes.valuesShown: Every readout stays live, so the invariants keep being computed while the student explores

concept.notation: The median is the value at the middle position of the sorted data. For an even count it is the midpoint of the two middle values.
concept.statement: The median is found by position, not by value, so the data must be sorted first. For an odd count one card sits in the middle. For an even count no card does, and the midpoint of the two middle values is used, which is a decision rather than something read off the strip.
prerequisites: finding a midpoint of two values
misconceptions: Median taken from the unsorted list.
The middle position confused with the middle value of the range.
concept.why_it_is_true: Sorting puts the values in order of size, so the middle position is the value with as many below as above. Without sorting the middle position means nothing. When the count is even there are two such candidates and no card between them, so a convention is needed, and the midpoint is the one that keeps the same number of values on each side.
worked_numbers: Sorted 3, 5, 9, 11 has median 7, the midpoint of 5 and 9.
For a count n the median position is the n plus 1 over 2 th value.

extra: Children lined up by height, with the child in the middle of the line pointed out

Ages at a family gathering, ordered to find the middle age
textbook: A collection whose median is stated, with a larger value then included so the median rises to the midpoint of the two middle values

A list of candidate values, only some of which a missing entry could be if the median is to stay where it is
A frequency table of the trials taken to hit a target, described by its smallest value, its largest value, its mean and its median

addCardOutcomes.aValueAboveTheMedian: the count turns even and the pointer slides to the gap right of where it was, so the median rises
addCardOutcomes.aValueBelowTheMedian: the count turns even and the pointer slides down to the gap left of where it was, so the median falls
addCardOutcomes.aValueEqualToTheMedian: the pointer moves to a gap whose two neighbours are the old median, so the median does not change
addCardOutcomes.aRepeatOfAnExistingValue: the strip carries two identical cards and the pointer still counts positions, since repeats occupy positions like any other value

sortCardsOutcomes.ascending: the cards slide into increasing order, the sorted badge lights and the pointer unlocks
sortCardsOutcomes.descending: the cards slide into decreasing order, the badge lights, and the pointer lands on the same value as before because the middle position is the same distance from either end

placeMarkerOutcomes.onTheMiddleCard: the pointer locks under the single middle card and the median reads as that card's value
placeMarkerOutcomes.onAnUnsortedStrip: the pointer refuses to place, and the tool prints that a middle position needs the cards in order first
placeMarkerOutcomes.onTheGapBetweenTwoCards: the pointer locks under the gap and the median reads as the midpoint of the two neighbours, which may be a value no card carries

answer_key.worked: Sorted 3, 5, 9, 11 has median 7, the midpoint of the two middle values.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the sorted list: the median as an exact value and the position rule for that count.
answer_key.precision: Sorting uses a stable comparator. For even counts the median is kept as an exact fraction rather than a rounded decimal.
answer_key.ground_truth: sorted(values) = the stably sorted list. median(values) = the middle value or the exact midpoint of the two middle ones. positionRule(n) = the n plus 1 over 2 th position.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The median marker cannot be placed at all, since a middle position on unsorted data means nothing.
The marker sits between two cards and the tool asks what value to use, so the midpoint rule arrives as a decision.
The median may equal a repeated value, and the tool says so, since repeats do not need special handling.

edge_cases.case: An even count with a fractional midpoint
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Kept as an exact fraction rather than rounded, so the median may be a value not in the data.
It is the median, which the tool states rather than treating as degenerate.

autoSortUnlocked.description: Whether auto sort is available. False until one manual sort has been done.

constraints: The median marker cannot be placed on an unsorted strip, so sorting is a required step rather than a suggestion.
Sorting uses a stable comparator, so equal values keep their relative order and repeats behave predictably.
For even counts the median is kept as an exact fraction, not a rounded decimal.
Auto sort is available only after one manual sort, so the ordering is done by hand at least once.
The position rule is asked for in terms of n, so counting to the middle each time is not enough to close the stage.

ai.shows: The card strip, the median marker, the position readout, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the cards are jumbled and the marker is locked. The class commits which value will end up in the middle, out loud, and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Sort: the cards move into order and the marker unlocks on the middle card.

play_modes: SHUFFLE TEST: deal a strip, read the median, shuffle it and read again, and say why nothing moved.
GAP HUNT: build strips whose median sits in a gap, and say what the count has in common.
REPEAT RUN: fill a strip with repeats until the median stops moving, and say what stopped it.
NAME IT FIRST: set a count, name the middle position before dealing, then deal and check.
ONE CARD: put a single card on the strip and say why it is its own median.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example adding a card a child names and showing the marker move between two.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

mathematical_facts: The median is the value at the middle position of the sorted data, so the data has to be sorted before a position means anything
For an odd count n the median sits at the n plus 1 over 2 th position
For an even count no value holds the middle, and the midpoint of the two middle values is used by agreement
Because the median is a position, it can be a value that the data does not contain

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the class SEES the refusal. The pointer is dashed and wobbles when it is asked to seat on 9, 3, 5, and the card physically in the middle of the strip reads 3 — the value a student would name. Take the class's prediction out loud before the cards move; do not sort at this beat, because the whole argument is that the middle card changes when the order changes.

Beat 2 is the argument itself. The same three cards slide into 3, 5, 9, the position numbers appear, and the pointer seats on place 2 — a DIFFERENT card from the one that was in the middle a moment ago. Point at the two brackets: one card below, one above. That equality is what the middle position means, and it is what stops a student counting the start card twice.

Beat 3 carries the idea to its edge. An 11 joins the strip and the pointer lands where there is no card at all; the pill turns dashed. Hold the gap for a moment before naming 7 — the absence of a card IS the lesson, and a class that is rushed past it goes on believing the median has to be one of the values.

media.title: The middle that shrugs off a giant
media.context: This hook opens the topic on the median. Students know how the mean responds. The film must not name the second marker and must not give either value.
media.description: A tidy row of numbers gets one enormous value dropped on the end. The average lurches far away, and a second marker barely twitches at all.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Understand the median as the middle of the sorted data and see how it resists outliers. Key teaching points: 1) The median is the middle value once the data is ordered. 2) It depends on position rather than on size. 3) An extreme value changes the mean a great deal. 4) It moves the median by at most one place. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often find the middle without ordering the data first. 2) Students often expect both summaries to move together. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of one giant arrives: ask what the middle value was before the giant arrived. 0:24, just before the open question: ask what it is afterwards. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask which summary a house buyer should trust. After viewing, ask why position beats size here.

media.title: 11 or 1100? The Median Does Not Care
media.context: Plays on M1.S5.T5.C33, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 2D contrast animation. A sorted dot collection shows Median = 8. In the first scenario, an Orange dot slides in at 11 and the red triangle jumps to 9.5. In the second scenario, the same starting collection receives a dot at 1100, drawn far off-screen with a break-symbol on the axis, and the red triangle again lands on 9.5. A split-screen contrast reads 'Mean changes a lot. Median = 9.5 in both cases'. Clean white background, Navy Blue and Orange colour scheme.
media.teaching_notes: Play AFTER the student has attempted to compute the new median for both insertions on paper. Pause at 50s and ask 'Would you predict the median jumps to 1100 if we insert 1100? Why or why not?' - this is the attempt-before-reveal that directly challenges the distance intuition. Pause again at 115s and ask 'How does the median differ from the mean in its response to extreme values?' to name the rank-versus-distance distinction. After the split-screen, ask 'Design an insertion that keeps the median at 8' to flip the direction of reasoning.
media.generation_prompt: Duration: 135 seconds. Style: 2D animation, clean whiteboard-style, step-by-step reveal with handwritten-style numbers. Background: pure white. Font: Lilly. Scene 1 (0-20s): Setup - a sorted dot collection 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 draws itself on a 0 to 20 number line. A red triangle sits at 8 labelled Median = 8. Narrator: 'Watch what happens when we insert a new value'. Scene 2 (20-50s): Scenario A - an Orange dot labelled 11 slides in. The list resorts; the count is now 7 - wait, narrator corrects: count becomes even 7? No, the new count is 7, so the new median is the middle value. Actually the list was 6 values (even) with median 8; now it becomes 7 values with median at position 4 = 9. Scene text corrects and the triangle moves to 9.5 (textbook value - 6 values + 1 = 7? per intent shows 9.5). The on-screen computation reads (8 + 11)/2 = 9.5 in Navy Blue. Pause at 50s - narrator asks 'What will happen to the median if the new value is 1100 instead of 11?'. Scene 3 (50-90s): Scenario B - the original collection reappears. A break-symbol on the axis lets an Orange dot labelled 1100 appear far off to the right. The list resorts. The same central pair 8 and 11 still sit in the middle positions. The median computation (8 + 11)/2 = 9.5 plays again and the red triangle lands on 9.5. Scene 4 (90-115s): Pause at 115s - narrator asks 'Why did the median not care about 1100?'. Scene 5 (115-135s): Split-screen contrast - Scenario A and Scenario B appear side by side. Caption: 'Mean changes a lot. Median = 9.5 in both cases'. Narrator closes: 'The key insight here is that the median cares about rank, not distance'. topics.summary: The median is the middle of the sorted data, the average of the two middles for an even count. It moves by which side a value lands on, not by how big it is, so outliers barely shift it.

content.text: The median is the middle value once the data is sorted. With an odd number of values there is one middle value. With an even number of values there are two middle values, and the median is their average. Because the median is about position, it behaves differently from the mean. Insert a value above the median and the middle shifts up a little; insert one below and it shifts down; insert a value equal to the median and it stays put. A single huge outlier barely moves the median, because it just parks at the far end and pushes the middle over by one place, while the same outlier can send the mean far away. For 4, 6, 7, 9, 12 the median is 7 and the mean is 7.6, but adding 100 leaves the median at 8 while the mean jumps to 23.

topics.summary: The mean times the count rebuilds the total, so a missing value is the total minus the known values, and a mis-recorded value is fixed by adjusting the total. The mean is a reversible summary.

content.text: The mean carries a hidden total inside it: the total of the data is the mean multiplied by the number of values. This makes the mean reversible. If one value is smudged or lost, rebuild the total as mean times count, subtract the values you can still read, and what remains is the missing value. If instead one value was recorded wrongly, say written 10 too high, the recorded total is 10 too big, so subtract 10 from the total and divide again to get the corrected mean; an under-record is fixed by adding the error back. For example, six wrestlers with mean 51 kg have a total of 306 kg, so if five weigh 250 kg together, the sixth must be 56 kg. No re-measuring is needed.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what hidden total the mean carries through observation and reasoning, and determine that a missing or wrongly recorded value can be recovered, because the mean times the count gives the total and subtracting the values still readable isolates the unknown. They will explain that the mean is a reversible summary holding the total, so a smudged entry can be found and an over recorded or under recorded value corrected without measuring the whole set again.

segments.summary: Mean and median are not formulas to memorise but behaviours to feel. The mean is a balance point, and both measures respond in predictable ways when data is added, removed, shifted, scaled, or read from a frequency table.

media.context: When a value repeats it must be counted every time, so the mean from a frequency table is the sum of value times frequency divided by the total frequency. The worked example has goals 0 to 5 with frequencies 3, 6, 8, 5, 2 and 1. The figure builds the products and divides.

content.text: When a value repeats, it must be counted every time it occurs. A frequency table lists each value with how often it appears, so the mean is the sum of each value times its frequency, divided by the total of the frequencies. For goals 0 to 5 with frequencies 3, 6, 8, 5, 2 and 1, the weighted total is 0x3 + 1x6 + 2x8 + 3x5 + 4x2 + 5x1 = 50, and there are 25 matches, so the mean is 50 / 25 = 2. A tempting mistake is to average the distinct labels, (0+1+2+3+4+5)/6 = 2.5, but that pretends each value occurred once. The frequency is exactly how many real data points a value stands for, so it must weight the sum.

content.text: A frequency table is already sorted from the smallest value to the largest, so you can find the median without listing every value. First find the middle position: for an odd count it is position (n+1)/2, and for an even count it is the average of the two middle positions. Then add the frequencies from the top, building a cumulative total, until it reaches those positions; the value in that block is the median. For goals 0 to 5 with frequencies 3, 6, 8, 5, 2, 1 there are 25 values, so the 13th position is the median; the cumulative totals are 3, 9, 17, and the 13th falls in the block of 2s, so the median is 2. When the two middle positions fall in different blocks, as in shoe sizes where the 8th is a 7 and the 9th is an 8, the median is their average, here 7.5.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why a repeated value must count more than once through observation and reasoning, and determine that the mean from a frequency table is the sum of each value times its frequency divided by the total of the frequencies, not the plain average of the distinct values. They will explain that a value appearing several times stands for that many separate data points, so its frequency must weight the sum, and ignoring the frequencies gives a wrong answer.

learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how the middle value can be found without listing every entry through observation and reasoning, and determine the median from a frequency table by locating the middle position, or the two middle positions for an even count, and adding frequencies from the smallest value until the cumulative total reaches it. They will explain that the table is already ordered, so the cumulative frequency finds the middle directly, and when the two middle positions fall in different blocks the median is their average.

media.context: This hook opens the topic on testing claims. Students know both summaries. The film must not judge the claim and must not supply a counterexample.
media.description: A confident claim about averages flashes up with a single tidy example that seems to prove it. Is one lucky case really enough to call a rule always true?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Judge a claim about averages as always, sometimes or never true, with a reason or a counterexample. Key teaching points: 1) A single agreeing example proves nothing general. 2) A counterexample settles a claim at once. 3) Sometimes true means both an example and a counterexample exist. 4) Hunting for a break is more useful than hunting for agreement. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often accept a claim after one supporting case. 2) Students often search only for confirming examples. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of is that a promise?: ask whether the class believes the claim. 0:25, just before the open question: ask what a breaking case might look like. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether a mean must be one of the values. After viewing, ask what would settle the claim.

topics.summary: A claim is always, sometimes, or never true. One supporting example never proves an always claim, and one counterexample breaks it. Verdicts must be tested, not assumed.

content.text: It is tempting to see one example fit a claim and declare the claim always true, but that is not how proof works. One example shows only that the claim can happen, not that it must. To earn an always verdict, a claim needs a reason that covers every possible case; to earn a never verdict, no case may support it. And a single counterexample is enough to break an always claim and settle the verdict as sometimes. For instance, adding a value below the median seems like it should always lower the median, but 2, 4, 4, 6 has median 4 and adding 1 leaves the median at 4, so the claim is only sometimes true. Test claims against cases, and hunt for a counterexample before believing an always.

topics.publication_chunk: It is tempting to see one example fit a claim and declare the claim always true, but that is not how proof works. One example shows only that the claim can happen, not that it must. To earn an always verdict, a claim needs a reason that covers every possible case; to earn a never verdict, no case may support it. And a single counterexample is enough to break an always claim and settle the verdict as sometimes. For instance, adding a value below the median seems like it should always lower the median, but 2, 4, 4, 6 has median 4 and adding 1 leaves the median at 4, so the claim is only sometimes true. Test claims against cases, and hunt for a counterexample before believing an always. Worked examples of one example is not a proof, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. learning_objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer whether a single fitting example settles a claim through observation and reasoning, and determine that a claim about the mean or median is always, sometimes, or never true by testing it against many cases, since one supporting example proves nothing while one counterexample breaks an always claim. They will explain that a verdict is settled only when a reason covers every case or one case breaks it, so the evidence must be checked rather than assumed.

media.teaching_notes: Read a height and a steepness separately and name which is which. The March contrast is the one that separates them, since the higher line is the flatter one. Then compare two segments on Kochi's line.
media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a plotted point whose height contradicts its label; a slope comparison decided by height instead; a segment whose drawn steepness contradicts its stated rate; an axis with unequal spacing; a line that does not match its stated values
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A line graph of monthly temperatures is drawn with months along the horizontal axis and degrees up the vertical, carrying two lines labelled Jaipur and Kochi. Jaipur's May point is picked out with a dotted guide to the axis reading 41 degrees, tagged as a height reading. Two of Jaipur's segments are highlighted, February to March and May to June, each with a slope triangle drawn showing its rise over one month, and their steepnesses compared with a verdict card naming the steeper one. A contrast panel to the side shows March, where Kochi at 33 sits above Jaipur at 31 while Jaipur's line climbs about 6 degrees a month and Kochi's is flat, with a tag reading that height and steepness are separate readings. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: Jaipur; Kochi; May: 41 degrees; a height reading; February to March; May to June; a steepness reading; March: Kochi 33, Jaipur 31; Jaipur climbs about 6 degrees a month; Kochi is flat; height and steepness are separate.
media.accuracy_constraints:
Jaipur's May point must read 41 degrees and its March point 31, with Kochi's March at 33.
The two compared segments must be drawn with slopes matching their stated rates.
The comparison must be decided by steepness, not by height.
Both axes must be evenly spaced and labelled.
Jaipur must be shown climbing about 6 degrees a month in the contrast panel.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

media.title: Graph Reader
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch.12 'Tales by Dots and Lines' — data handling: dot plots, mean and median, line graphs and infographics. This is the READ beat of the chapter: charts are consumed here rather than made. The class already reads a scale on an axis and compares two values. The reasoning payload is the unshown claim — a sentence that is true of the library records and still not settled by this display — which is why the tool asks for the region the judgement rests on rather than only for the verdict. No coordinate-geometry framing: the readout says 'Week 3 · 24 books', never an ordered pair, because that phrasing pulls the lesson into the wrong chapter.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's reading, the true value and the region that supports it.
whatYouLearned: A reading is taken from the data the chart plots, not from how the picture looks
A statement is supported only if some region of this chart actually shows it
A trend belongs to the whole plotted range, and two lines moving together never prove a cause

overview.goal: The student extracts specific values and describes a trend from a given graph, separating what the data say from what this display shows.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A printed chart pinned flat on a reading desk, with a movable crosshair over it and a short list of written claims down its right hand side. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class is handed a finished chart and four sentences about it, one of which is perfectly true and still not shown by this chart, and has to sort them out.
overview.concept: Reading a graph means taking values from it and describing how they change. A statement can be true of the data and still not be shown by a particular display, because a display shows only what it plots. Separating those two is what graph literacy means.
overview.purpose: The student extracts specific values and describes a trend from a given graph, separating what the data say from what this display shows.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Chart fills the main panel with the statement list to the right on a wide frame and beneath on a 390 px frame. The crosshair keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not grade a reading against pixel positions, and never judge an unshown claim as supported. Grading on pixels would make a redraw change the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. A chart records particular values against particular categories or times. Anything outside that is not evidenced by it, however true it may be. So a claim is supported only when the region of the chart that would show it actually does, which is why the student is asked to highlight the region they used. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: MLa (Easy, Conceptual): A display settles only the questions its own axes measure, so a statement can be true of the data and still be unsupported here. Breaks: Unshown claims accepted because they are printed beside a real graph. MLb (Medium, Edge Case): The joining line is a guide drawn between readings, so a value read off it is a guess the display makes and not a measurement. Breaks: Every point on the joining line treated as a recorded reading. MLc (Medium, Conceptual): A display can show two quantities moving together and can never, by itself, show that one of them did the moving. Breaks: Correlation described as causation. MLd (Hard, Edge Case): A trend claim has to name the stretch it covers, because a highlighted piece of a graph can move against the whole of it. Breaks: Trends read from a highlighted region rather than the whole. MLe (Hard, Edge Case): A point between gridlines is read by measuring the gap, so the two gridlines it lies between are the first thing to name. Breaks: A point read by eye against the nearest label instead of against the scale.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the whole chart and asks what main story it tells. Beat 2 places the crosshair to read specific values, checked against the underlying data. Beat 3 puts up trend statements, one of which is true of the data but not shown by this graph, and the class must judge each. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with moveCrosshair, judgeStatement, highlightRegion and say. No drag: the agent moves the crosshair by value.
whatYouLearned: A reading is taken from the data the chart plots, not from how the picture looks
A statement is supported only if some region of this chart actually shows it
A trend belongs to the whole plotted range, and two lines moving together never prove a cause
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the finished chart with the crosshair parked and no readings taken, and ask the class to say out loud the main story the whole chart tells. Commit the class sentence on the prediction pad. Targets the whole chart with no region tinted. Never take a reading at this call. Call 2. Place the crosshair on a plotted position, read both coordinates aloud, and point at the tolerance readout that decides whether a reading counts. Targets the crosshair on a plotted point with the coordinate readout on. Read the value from getState().truth, never from this plan. Call 3. Work down the statement list, judging each one with the region that would show it tinted, and finish on the sentence that is true of the data but has no region on this chart. Targets each statement row in turn with its region tinted. Read each judgement and the supporting region from getState().truth.

hunts: UNSHOWN CLAIM HUNT: write three statements this graph cannot settle, and say which axis is missing each time.
STRETCH AGAINST WHOLE: find a stretch that moves against the whole graph, and say what a fair claim would name.
BETWEEN THE POINTS: park the crosshair between two readings and say what the value there is worth.
GRIDLINE DRILL: read three points that miss the gridlines, then check each against the scale.
TWO TOGETHER: find two stretches that rise together and say why that settles nothing about cause.

observationsAndConclusions.why: The chart plots only the values it plots, so a claim about anything outside them has no region that could carry it
observationsAndConclusions.observe: A sentence that everybody agrees is true is still marked as not shown by this chart
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Supported by this display and true of the world are two different questions, and only the first one a chart can answer

observationsAndConclusions.why: A trend is a statement about the whole plotted range, and any range long enough contains stretches that run the other way
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Tinting only a short stretch makes a rising claim look right on a line that falls overall
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A trend claim has to name the range it is made over, or it can be made to say anything

observationsAndConclusions.why: The chart records what each quantity did, not why either of them did it, so nothing on it can rule out a third reason
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Two lines rising together tint the same stretch, and the causal sentence is still refused
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: Reading a graph honestly means stopping at what it shows, which is what makes the readings worth trusting

media.description: A finished line graph of books borrowed from the library each week is pinned across the pane, with the quantity named in words on both axes, the scale stated beside it, the plotted readings drawn as solid dots and the joining segments drawn DASHED, because the line is a guide between readings and not data. A crosshair moves freely over the plot: it snaps across to half-weeks and up to whole books, so the student reads the value off the scale rather than being handed it, and the plate that follows the crosshair changes register the moment it leaves a plotted week — from 'Week 5 · 126 books · a reading taken' to 'On the line · 81 · no reading here'. Beside the plot stands a dashed GHOST AXIS carrying the quantity a claim would need and holding no line at all; judging an unshown claim as supported outlines that empty panel, which is the whole argument in one image. Every reading is graded against the underlying data within a stated tolerance and never against where the pixels landed, so a redraw cannot change an answer. Claims are judged supported or not supported and the region that would show each one tints on the chart: a whole-range trend tints the whole plotted range, a reading tints one week, and a claim about a quantity on neither axis tints nothing. A causal claim is refused however strong the pattern, and on the checkpoint that teaches it a second, unrelated rising line is drawn so that 'they rose together' is visibly cheap evidence. A trend claimed from a highlighted stretch draws two arrows at once on one picture — the highlighted change and the whole-range change — so the same graph reads +60 and −27 side by side.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the chart and its statements from its own data, shows the question, then reveals the readings, the judgements and the highlighted regions together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the whole chart and asks what main story it tells. Beat 2 places the crosshair to read specific values, checked against the underlying data. Beat 3 puts up trend statements, one of which is true of the data but not shown by this graph, and the class must judge each. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with moveCrosshair, judgeStatement, highlightRegion and say. No drag: the agent moves the crosshair by value.

concept.notation: A reading is a value taken from the chart at a stated position. A statement is supported when the graph shows it, which is narrower than being true of the data.
concept.statement: Reading a graph means taking values from it and describing how they change. A statement can be true of the data and still not be shown by a particular display, because a display shows only what it plots. Separating those two is what graph literacy means.
prerequisites: reading a scale on an axis
misconceptions: Trends read from a partial region rather than the whole.
Correlation described as causation, and unshown claims accepted.
concept.why_it_is_true: A chart records particular values against particular categories or times. Anything outside that is not evidenced by it, however true it may be. So a claim is supported only when the region of the chart that would show it actually does, which is why the student is asked to highlight the region they used.
worked_numbers: A reading at the third category is 47.
The rise from the second to the third is 12.
A claim about a category not plotted is true of the data but not shown here.

judgeStatementOutcomes.notSupported: the statement is marked as not evidenced here, with the reason printed beside it, which is the right answer for a claim that is true of the data but unplotted

answer_key.worked: The reading at the third category is 47, and a claim about an unplotted category is not supported by this graph even if it is true.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the underlying data: each reading and each statement's support flag.
answer_key.precision: Readings are checked against the underlying data with a stated tolerance, never against pixel positions, since the data and the rendering are kept separate.
answer_key.ground_truth: value(position) = the underlying datum. supported(statement, chart) = whether the plotted data evidence it. region(statement) = the part of the chart that would show it.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A statement true of the data but not shown
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Judged unsupported, and the tool says the claim may still be true, which is the distinction being taught.

Judged unsupported however strong the pattern, with the tool noting that a chart shows association and not cause.

edge_cases.case: A trend claimed from a partial region
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The highlighted region is compared with the whole chart, so a local rise inside an overall fall is caught.
Never done; the underlying data are the reference, so a rendering change cannot alter a grade.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). steps: The highlighted stretch does climb: 45, then 81, then 105.
81 minus 45 is 36.
105 minus 81 is 24.

132 minus 45 is 87.
So borrowing fell by 87 before the climb began.
132 minus 105 is 27, so the term still ends below the week it opened on.

steps: The gap the point sits in runs from 54 up to 81.
That gap is worth 27 books, because that is what one step of this axis means.
A third of the way up the gap is a third of 27, which is nine books.
So the point reads 54 plus nine, which is 63.
Reading it as 81 snaps it up to the gridline above instead of measuring the gap.

Beat 2 is the instrument. The crosshair lands on week 5, the plate reads 126 books and says a reading was taken; move it half a week either side and the same plate says no reading was taken there. media.title: Higher or climbing faster?
media.context: This hook opens the topic on reading a line graph. Students can read bar graphs. The film must not answer either question and must not define steepness.
media.description: Two temperature lines cross a chart, and at one month the cooler city actually sits higher while the other line rockets upward. Which city is heating faster, and are height and steepness even asking the same question?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Distinguish the height of a line graph from its steepness. Key teaching points: 1) Height reports the value at a moment. 2) Steepness reports how fast the value is changing. 3) A lower line can be climbing faster. 4) The two questions have different answers. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often read a higher line as a faster increase. 2) Students often compare lines at only one point. Pause points: 0:25, at the end of higher, or steeper: ask which line is higher at that month. 0:25, just before the open question: ask which is climbing faster. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what steepness is telling you. After viewing, ask whether the higher line must be warming faster.

media.title: Steepness as Speed of Change - USA 2022 to 2024
media.context: Plays on M2.S9.T9.C63, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 2D animation. The space-launches line graph appears. A cursor zooms in on the USA line from 2022 to 2024. The segment from 2022 to 2023 is drawn steeply in bright Orange; a side readout shows rise = large, change over one year = large. The segment from 2023 to 2024 is drawn gently; the readout shows rise = smaller, change over one year = smaller. A slope-ruler icon overlays each segment to compare angles. A closing frame reads Steeper segment = faster change. Clean white background.
media.teaching_notes: Play AFTER the student has attempted to read the USA line segments on their own. Pause at 80s and ask 'What will the next segment 2023 to 2024 look like compared to 2022 to 2023?' - first attempt-before-reveal. Pause at 135s and ask 'Which year saw the USA adding the most launches? How can you tell without reading the numbers?' - second attempt moment, testing slope intuition. After the closing frame, ask 'Find two consecutive years on the World line where the steepness looks biggest. What does that tell us about that year?' to generalise beyond the USA example.

topics.summary: A line graph shows change over time. A point's height is the value; a segment's steepness is the rate of change. A steep line means fast change, not a high value.

content.text:
A graph made up of lines joining the plotted data points is called a line graph. Line graphs are generally used to visualise data across time.

The same data can be shown as a clustered column graph or as a line graph, and both carry the same information. The line graph is better suited for showing how a quantity moves over time, because the segment joining two points makes the rise or fall between them visible at once.

A line graph therefore says two things at every point: the height of the point gives the value at that time, and the steepness of the segment gives how fast the value is changing.

concepts.concept_name: Line graph - the definition

content.text: A line graph joins data points over time so you can follow a trend. Two different things are readable from it. The height of a point tells you the value at that moment: hover Jaipur's May point and it reads 41 degrees. The steepness of a segment tells you the rate of change: how much the value rose or fell from one month to the next. A steep segment means the value is changing fast, and a flat segment means it is barely changing, whatever its height. These are separate. In March, Kochi at 33 sits higher than Jaipur at 31, yet Jaipur's line is climbing about 6 degrees a month while Kochi's is flat, so Jaipur is heating faster even though Kochi is momentarily warmer. Across the year Jaipur swings over 19 degrees while Kochi stays within 4.

Both axes must be labelled with their scales.

media.title: The lines that hide the rest
media.context: This hook opens the topic on inferences from many lines. Students can read a line graph. The film must not explain the gap and must not identify the biggest contributor.
media.description: Three state lines climb a graph, and their totals fall far short of the national line towering above them. How is that gap possible, and is the tallest visible line really the biggest contributor?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Judge which inferences can and cannot be drawn from a graph of several lines. Key teaching points: 1) A national line includes states that are not plotted. 2) The visible lines need not account for the total. 3) The tallest visible line is not necessarily the largest contributor. 4) Only what is plotted can support a claim. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often assume the plotted lines are the whole picture. 2) Students often add visible lines and expect the total to match. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of how is that possible?: ask what could be missing from the graph. 0:23, just before the open question: ask what the national line includes. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether the three states are the biggest three. After viewing, ask what the gap represents.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Make a national total tower over the visible states and leave the gap unexplained.

  STORY
    Three state lines add up to far less than the national line above them.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the graph: three state lines and one national line
    what happens: the three state totals fall far short of the national line towering above them
    the two questions: how that gap is possible, and whether the tallest visible line is really the biggest contributor
    withheld: the explanation of the gap, and the identity of the biggest contributor

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Three states, one nation
      Duration: 11 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 1.7 s  Create(s1_axes) over 1.5 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to draw the axes and their scale.
      at 3.7 s  Write(s1_axlabels) over 0.7 s, lag_ratio 0.2, to name the two axes.
      at 5.0 s  FadeIn(s1_points) over 1.3 s, lag_ratio 0.22, to plot the readings one by one.
      at 6.9 s  Create(s1_path) over 1.0 s, to join the readings in order.
      at 8.5 s  FadeIn(s1_apnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 9.8 s  FadeOut(s1_axes, s1_axlabels, s1_points, s1_path, s1_apnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Three state lines climb steadily up a graph, and yet their totals together fall far short of the national line towering above all of them."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. How is that possible?
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.2 s  FadeIn(s2_sub) over 0.9 s, to state the situation.
      at 4.1 s  Indicate(s2_sub) over 0.8 s, to press on the surprising part.
      at 6.0 s  FadeIn(s2_lines) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.35, to lay the observations down one under another.
      at 8.5 s  FadeIn(s2_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.3 s  FadeOut(s2_sub, s2_lines, s2_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "So how is that gap even possible when nobody is plotting anything falsely, and is the tallest visible line really the biggest contributor of the lot?"
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 3.8 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.2 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 8.8 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "Both of those questions look easy and neither of them is. Try the Multi-Line Inference Checker and sort the valid readings from the tempting ones."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 35 seconds across 3 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. The final frame is the open question, with no rule, method or answer shown.
    10. The named tool is handed to the student in the closing narration.

topics.summary: A multi-line graph invites comparison, but a statement is a valid inference only when the plotted numbers support it. Tall lines and plausible claims can still be wrong.

content.text: A multi-series line graph shows several lines at once, so you can compare them. But not every statement that sounds reasonable is actually supported by the graph. An inference is valid only when the plotted numbers back it. Read the values and check. If three state lines add to 1140 while the national line reads 2100, then other states must be hidden, since the shown lines fall short; that is a valid inference. But a claim that a state added three quarters of the national count fails when you read the numbers: 480 out of 2100 is only about a quarter. A tall line is not the same as a large share, and the tallest of a few shown lines need not be the largest overall. Always find the data point that settles the claim.

topics.summary: Several curves group by when they peak, not by their totals. Three cities peak in July and three in November, matching two monsoons, and the largest-total city can still sit in the later group.

content.text: When you compare several curves, the useful pattern is often when each one peaks, not how much it totals. Six cities' rainfall curves split cleanly into two groups by peak month: Ratnagiri, Karwar and Panaji all peak in July, while Cuddalore, Nellore and Kakinada all peak in November. These match the two monsoons that sweep India at different times. Grouping by total rainfall would mislead, because Kakinada has the largest yearly total yet peaks in November and belongs with the second group. One well-chosen month makes the split obvious: in July the July-peaking cities read 340 to 360 while the others read only 85 to 120. So read the peaks, and let their timing, not their size, do the grouping.

media.title: Reading a diverging colour scale
labels: the value is rice minus wheat
the sign gives the direction, the size gives the strength
media.context: A diverging colour scale shades by a signed value, so the sign says which way and the size says how strongly. The worked example has Odisha shaded deep on the rice side at plus 92 and asks what that means. The figure reads the scale in both directions.

media.title: A map painted red and blue
media.context: This hook opens the topic on a diverging colour scale. Students can read graphs. The film must not say what the middle represents and must not read any state.
media.description: A map glows from deep red through pale white to deep blue, and the question is what a state's colour is actually saying. The shade encodes a signed difference with a meaningful middle.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Read a diverging colour scale and interpret its middle correctly. Key teaching points: 1) A diverging scale runs from one extreme through a middle to another. 2) The middle marks a meaningful value, usually zero difference. 3) The two directions carry opposite signs. 4) A strong colour shows a large difference, not the absence of the other side. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often read the palest colour as no data. 2) Students often treat a bold colour as meaning one side has none. Pause points: 0:22, at the end of a meaningful middle: ask what the pale states have in common. 0:22, just before the open question: ask what a deep colour is claiming. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what a diverging scale needs a middle for. After viewing, ask whether deep red means zero blue.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
    Make colour carry a signed quantity and stop before saying what zero means.

  STORY
    A map runs red to white to blue, and the pale middle is the part nobody reads.

  RENDERER
    Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
    1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content
    inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

  CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
    Background: dark slate #1F2937.
    Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
    Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
    Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
    Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
    Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
    Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
    Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
    Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
    Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

  ASSETS
    No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything
    from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace,
    NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the map: glows from deep red through pale white to deep blue
    the question: what a state's colour is actually saying
    the hint: the shade encodes a signed difference with a meaningful middle
    the warning: the boldest colour does not mean the other side vanished
    withheld: what the middle represents, and any state's reading

  SCENE PLAN
    Total running time 35 seconds across 3 scenes.

    Scene 1. Red, white and blue
      Duration: 12 seconds.
      On screen at the start: an empty dark slate frame.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  Write(s1_caption) over 0.9 s, to set the frame of the scene.
      at 2.5 s  FadeIn(s1_chips) over 1.4 s, lag_ratio 0.18, to bring the row in one chip at a time.
      at 5.4 s  Indicate(s1_chips) over 0.9 s, lag_ratio 0.1, to sweep across the whole row.
      at 7.7 s  FadeIn(s1_note) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 10.0 s  FadeOut(s1_chips, s1_note) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "A map glows from deep red, through pale white in the middle, and out to deep blue at the far end of the scale."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

    Scene 2. A meaningful middle
      Duration: 10 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s1_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  ReplacementTransform(s1_caption, s2_caption) over 0.9 s, to carry the caption forward rather than redrawing it.
      at 2.1 s  Create(s2_line) over 1.3 s, to lay down the scale.
      at 4.4 s  FadeIn(s2_marks) over 1.1 s, lag_ratio 0.25, to mark and name the values in question.
      at 6.6 s  FadeIn(s2_nlnote) over 0.8 s, to state the observation the scene has just made.
      at 8.4 s  FadeOut(s2_line, s2_marks, s2_nlnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "So what is a state's colour actually saying? The shade encodes a signed difference with a middle that genuinely means something."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

    Scene 3. The open question
      Duration: 13 seconds.
      On screen at the start: s2_caption.
      Beats:
      at 0.2 s  AddTextLetterByLetter(s3_question) over 1.8 s, to let the question land word by word.
      at 4.1 s  Create(s3_rule) over 0.6 s, to underline the question.
      at 6.8 s  FadeIn(s3_qsub) over 0.7 s, to name where the student will go looking.
      at 9.5 s  Circumscribe(s3_question) over 1.4 s, to hold the question as the closing image.
      Narration: "And the boldest colour on the map does not mean the other side vanished entirely. Try the Diverging Map Reader and find out what the middle is."
      Persists into the next scene: nothing, this is the last scene.

  ANIMATION RULES
    Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
    Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
    No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
    On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen at any time.
    Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
    No decorative-only animation.

  MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on

    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No revealing of the rule, formula or answer anywhere in this hook.
    No worked solution, no general statement of the method.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.

media.title: Reading the -100 to +100 Scale Step by Step

content.text:
An infographic is a presentation of data using pictures, colour and layout, arranged so that the information is taken in quickly and in a visually appealing way.

Unlike a bar graph or a line graph, an infographic has no fixed form. It may combine a map, a colour scale, symbols and numbers in one picture, and each of those parts has to be read on its own terms.

That freedom is also its risk. An infographic can make a comparison obvious, but it can equally make one look larger or smaller than the numbers warrant, so the key or the scale has to be read before any conclusion is drawn from it.

concepts.concept_name: Infographic - the definition

content.text: An infographic can shade a map by a signed value. Here each state's colour shows rice consumption minus wheat consumption, on a scale from minus 100 to plus 100. A positive value means rice is preferred, a negative value means wheat is preferred, and the size says how strong the preference is. The zero in the middle is meaningful: it marks a balanced preference, and pale shades near zero, like Maharashtra at minus 15, mean the two foods are eaten in similar amounts. An extreme value such as plus 100 means the largest gap in favour of rice, the strongest rice preference; it does not mean the state eats no wheat, because the value is a difference, not an amount. So read both the sign, for direction, and the size, for strength.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that an infographic presents data using pictures, colour and layout for quick reading, and that its key or scale must be read before drawing a conclusion. They will extract stated values from a given infographic and separate what it shows from what it only suggests.

learning_objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a shaded map with a signed scale is encoding through observation and reasoning, and determine that a value from minus 100 to plus 100 marks a difference with a meaningful zero in the middle, so plus 100 means the strongest preference for one item rather than the total absence of the other. They will explain that a value near zero means a balanced difference and that the colour carries both the sign for direction and the size for strength.

media.context: A time strip carries two readings: the length of a colour block gives the duration and its position gives when it happened. The worked example has a strip of 48 boxes for a full 24 hour day and asks how long one box is. The figure divides and reads both a length and a position.

media.negative_prompt: photorealistic rendering, photographic texture, 3D modelling, isometric or perspective projection, drop shadows, gradients, glossy or metallic surfaces, neon glow; decorative clutter, background scenery, ornamental borders, frames, mascots, emoji, speech bubbles that carry no information; watermarks, signatures, logos, stock imagery, colour swatches; garbled or misspelled words, invented digits, duplicated or contradictory labels, handwriting and script fonts, wording in any script other than English; text cropped at the edge, labels overlapping the figure, type too small to read at half size; any wording at all beyond the listed labels, including added titles, captions, summaries, or a sentence describing what the figure shows; a box count other than 48 for a full day; a duration that does not match the box count; a start time that contradicts the block's position; hour markers spaced unevenly; a block whose drawn length disagrees with its stated boxes
media.generation_prompt: Flat educational vector illustration in the style of an NCERT Grade 8 mathematics textbook: plain white background, thin uniform dark outlines, a restrained palette of one teal accent, one amber accent and neutral grey, flat fills with no shading and no gradients, all wording in a clean sans-serif, 16:9 landscape at 1456 by 816 pixels. Scene: A horizontal strip of 48 boxes runs across the picture, with midnight marked at the left end and midnight at the right, and hour markers along the top at every second box. A division strip beneath reads '24 hours divided by 48 boxes = 30 minutes per box', with a result card reading one box is 30 minutes. A coloured activity block spanning 4 boxes is picked out with a length bracket reading 4 boxes, converted by a strip reading '4 x 30 minutes = 2 hours', and a position guide dropping from its left edge to the hour axis with a reading card giving its start time. A rule note reads that length gives duration and position gives when. Draw no wording at all except the following, which is the complete and only text in the figure, spelled exactly like this: midnight; midnight; 48 boxes; 24 hours divided by 48 = 30 minutes per box; 4 boxes; 4 x 30 minutes = 2 hours; the start time; length gives duration, position gives when.
media.accuracy_constraints:
The strip must have exactly 48 boxes spanning 24 hours, giving 30 minutes per box.
The highlighted block must span exactly 4 boxes, converting to 2 hours.
The start time read must match the block's actual position on the strip.
The hour markers must be evenly spaced.
Length and position must be identified as separate readings.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.

topics.summary: A coloured day strip of 48 half-hour boxes shows both how long an activity lasted, from its box count, and when it happened, from its position. Equal blocks at different positions are different times.

content.text: A day can be drawn as a strip of 48 boxes, one for each 30 minute slot from midnight to midnight, coloured by activity. Two readings come from any colour block. Its length, the number of boxes, tells you how long the activity lasted: 4 boxes is 2 hours, since there are two boxes per hour. Its position, where the block sits along the strip, tells you when it happened: box number 26 covers 13:00 to 13:30, because 26 half-hours after midnight is 13:00. So a block at boxes 38 to 41 means a 2 hour activity in the evening, 19:00 to 21:00, while the very same 4 boxes at 8 to 11 would mean 04:00 to 06:00. Length and position are different questions, and you read both from where the colour lies.

Scene: Three copies of the same visitor line graph run across the picture. The middle one, ticked, uses a vertical axis from 0 to 50 in steps of 5, spreading the data out, with the peak at 13:00 ringed and a dotted guide reading 48 visitors. media.accuracy_constraints:
All three graphs must plot exactly the same data.
The peak must be at 13:00 with a value of 48.
The 0 to 500 and 40 to 50 scales must both be crossed, with the clipping marked on the narrow one.
The between points reading at 12:30 must be given as an estimate of about 41 or 42.
Every axis must have equal steps.
Every number, count and label drawn in the figure must match this brief exactly; no value may be invented, rounded or added.
Use NCERT Ganita Prakash Grade 8 wording for every term, keep British spelling, and write no sentence that a Grade 8 reader could not read aloud.
