media.title: The scale that flattens a story
media.context: This hook opens the topic on choosing a scale. Students can read line graphs. The film must not say which scale is fair and must not read any value between points.
media.description: The same visitor data is drawn twice, once lively and once nearly flat, purely by changing the axis. How can one honest dataset look so different, and can you even read a value sitting between two plotted points?
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Choose a scale honestly and judge what can be read between plotted points. Key teaching points: 1) The axis range changes the apparent size of a change. 2) A graph starting from zero shows true proportions. 3) Values between plotted points were never measured. 4) Joining points suggests values that may not exist. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often read a value off a joining line as though it were data. 2) Students often assume any drawn graph is scaled fairly. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of and what about between?: ask which of the two graphs the class believes. 0:24, just before the open question: ask what the joining line is actually claiming. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask where a bar graph should start. After viewing, ask whether a line between points is data.

media.title: Walking the Sleep Curve from Age 6 to 75
media.context: Plays on M2.S14.T14.C90, a concept of its own that exists to carry this video. A rendered animation delivered from the manim video library.
media.description: A 2D animation. The Sleepy-Deepy curve draws itself left to right. At age 6 a horizontal dashed line reads 9.5 hours on the vertical axis. The tracer drops to age 12 (about 9 hours), then to age 25 (about 8.3 hours), then to the trough region 30-50 (about 8 hours), then climbs past 50 to 8.5 at age 65. A side label throughout reads A curve that falls, flattens, rises - a U-like pattern. Clean white background, muted Navy Blue and Orange colour scheme.
media.teaching_notes: Play BEFORE the student attempts to read their own age on the sleep curve. Pause at 70s and ask 'What value do you expect at age 12?' - first attempt-before-reveal, testing interpolation. Pause at 120s and ask 'What name would you give this shape? Why?' - second attempt, targeting shape-naming mnemonics. After the closing label, ask 'Does the curve say every single 25-year-old sleeps 8.3 hours? Why or why not?' to lock the ERROR ALERT about average trends versus individuals.

It starts at (6, 9.5), drops gently through the teens, flattens between 30 and 50, and rises slightly past 50. Scene 3 (45-70s): Checkpoint 1 - a horizontal dashed line drops from age 6 on the horizontal axis to the curve and across to 9.5 on the vertical axis. A tooltip in Orange reads 'Age 6 - 9.5 h'. topics.topic_name: Figure it Out: scales and reading graphs
topics.brief_summary: A scale fitted to the data's range reveals the trend; too wide flattens it and too narrow clips it. A line graph also lets you estimate values between plotted points.
topics.original_chunk: How a line graph looks depends on the axis scale you choose, and the scale is a choice that can clarify or mislead. Fit the vertical scale to the data's range: for visitor counts from 12 to 48, a 0 to 50 axis in steps of 5 spreads the data out so the rise to a 13:00 peak and the fall after are clear. A scale that is far too wide, like 0 to 500, squashes the whole line near the bottom and makes a lively dataset look flat. A scale that is too narrow, like 40 to 50, clips off every value below 40. A line graph also lets you read between the plotted points: the connecting segment estimates in-between values, so at 12:30 the count is about halfway between 35 and 48, roughly 41 or 42. That is an estimate, not an exact measurement. Worked examples of choosing a scale, and reading between points, demonstrated one step at a time across different cases. media.title: Where the Middle Sits, and What Moves It
media.context: This is the chapter summary and it plays after the final topic. Every claim it makes has already been taught and practised, so nothing new appears and no fresh dataset is analysed. Its job is to extend the suspicion from summaries to graphs.
media.description: The film gathers the chapter together. The mean is a balance point, so every value tugs on it and one extreme value can drag it away from the crowd, while the median cares only about the middle position and shrugs outliers off.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Restate the chapter's conclusions about the mean, the median, frequencies and graphs. Key teaching points: 1) The mean is a balance point affected by every value. 2) Shifting and scaling change the mean predictably. 3) The median depends on position and resists outliers. 4) A missing value can be recovered from a known mean. 5) Axis, scale and colour shape what a graph appears to say. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often use the mean whatever the data looks like. 2) Students often trust a graph without checking its axis. Pause points: 0:32, at the end of shift it, or stretch it: ask which summary survives an outlier. 1:16, just before where the middle sits: ask which of the four cards they would explain first. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what a balance point means. After viewing, ask what they check first on a graph.

  MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
    Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.
    the mean: a balance point, so every value tugs on it and one extreme value can drag it away from the crowd
    shifting: add the same amount to every value and the mean shifts by that amount
    scaling: multiply them all and the mean scales, which makes it predictable under change
    the median: cares only about the middle position, so it shrugs off outliers and often describes a group more fairly
    frequencies: handle large sets
    an unknown value: can be recovered from a known mean

      Narration: "The mean is a balance point, so every single value in the set tugs on it, and one extreme value on its own can drag the whole thing well away from where the crowd actually sits."
      Persists into the next scene: s1_caption.

      Beats:

      at 12.4 s  FadeOut(s2_table, s2_tnote) over 0.6 s, lag_ratio 0.05, to clear the frame, keeping only what carries on.
      Narration: "Add the same amount to every value and the mean shifts by exactly that amount, and multiply them all and it scales in the same way, which makes it thoroughly predictable under change."
      Persists into the next scene: s2_caption.

      Duration: 15 seconds.

    100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct
    notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8
    textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a
    figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may
    pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

  LANGUAGE
    British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on
    screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places
    for any person or setting.

  NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
    No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
    No new content: every idea shown has already been taught in the chapter.
    No new worked example and no extension beyond the chapter.
    No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
    No external assets, watermarks or branding.
    No particles, sparkles or glow.

  SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT
    1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
    2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
    3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
    4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
    5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
    6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
    7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
    8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
    9. Every idea shown has already been taught inside the chapter; nothing is new.
    10. The conclusions are stated plainly and no fresh worked example appears.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that the mean is the sum of the values divided by number of values, also called the average or arithmetic mean, that the median is the middle value of the sorted data, and that the mean is a measure of central tendency. They will compute both for a given set of values.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what makes a point the true centre of a data set through observation and reasoning, and determine that the mean is the single place where the total distance to the values below it equals the total distance to the values above it, not the midpoint of the smallest and largest. They will explain that this balance point is unique, since sliding it either way makes one side heavier than the other.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of the mean is a balance point, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the mean is a balance point, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what happens to the balance point when a value joins or leaves a data set through observation and reasoning, and determine that a value above the current mean pulls it up, a value below pulls it down, and a value equal to it leaves it fixed, with removing a value doing the reverse. They will explain that the direction depends only on where the value sits relative to the mean, not on the act of adding or removing.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of adding or removing a value moves the mean, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving adding or removing a value moves the mean, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer when a change to the data leaves the mean exactly where it was through observation and reasoning, and determine that the mean holds still when the inserted or removed values contribute equal total distance above and below it, such as two values below balanced by one value far enough above. They will explain that the pull on each side cancels only when the added values share the same mean as the data, so values all on one side must move it.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what adding the same number to every value does to the centre through observation and reasoning, and determine that adding a fixed number to each value raises the mean by that number and subtracting a fixed number lowers it by that number, with no need to add the whole set again. They will explain that the total grows by the count times the added number while the count itself stays the same, so the mean shifts by exactly that number.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what multiplying every value by the same number does to the centre through observation and reasoning, and determine that multiplying each value by a number multiplies the mean by that same number, so doubling every value doubles the mean and halving every value halves it. They will explain that scaling each value scales the whole total while the count of values stays the same, so the mean scales by exactly that factor.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what value sits at the centre of sorted data through observation and reasoning, and determine that the median is the middle value once the data is ordered, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even, moving up or down only by which side a new value lands on. They will explain that the median answers to position rather than size, so a far outlier barely shifts it even though the same outlier strongly shifts the mean.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of the median is the middle of the sorted data, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the median is the middle of the sorted data, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what hidden total the mean carries through observation and reasoning, and determine that a missing or wrongly recorded value can be recovered, because the mean times the count gives the total and subtracting the values still readable isolates the unknown. They will explain that the mean is a reversible summary holding the total, so a smudged entry can be found and an over recorded or under recorded value corrected without measuring the whole set again.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer why a repeated value must count more than once through observation and reasoning, and determine that the mean from a frequency table is the sum of each value times its frequency divided by the total of the frequencies, not the plain average of the distinct values. They will explain that a value appearing several times stands for that many separate data points, so its frequency must weight the sum, and ignoring the frequencies gives a wrong answer.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how the middle value can be found without listing every entry through observation and reasoning, and determine the median from a frequency table by locating the middle position, or the two middle positions for an even count, and adding frequencies from the smallest value until the cumulative total reaches it. They will explain that the table is already ordered, so the cumulative frequency finds the middle directly, and when the two middle positions fall in different blocks the median is their average.

objectives.strand_name: The Balancing Act: mean and median
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer whether a single fitting example settles a claim through observation and reasoning, and determine that a claim about the mean or median is always, sometimes, or never true by testing it against many cases, since one supporting example proves nothing while one counterexample breaks an always claim. They will explain that a verdict is settled only when a reason covers every case or one case breaks it, so the evidence must be checked rather than assumed.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that a graph joining plotted points with line segments is called a line graph and that it is generally used for data across time, and distinguish the height of a point from the steepness of a segment. They will read a value and describe a change from a given line graph.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what two separate things a line graph reveals about a quantity over time through observation and reasoning, and determine that the height of a point gives the value at that moment while the steepness of a segment gives the rate of change, so a steeper part means a faster change rather than a higher value. They will explain that a nearly flat line means a quantity barely changing, so slope and height carry different information.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of reading a line graph: height versus steepness, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving reading a line graph: height versus steepness, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer which statements a graph with several lines actually supports through observation and reasoning, and determine that an inference holds only when the plotted numbers back it, so lines falling short of a total mean other contributors are hidden while a tall line can still be a small share of the whole. They will explain that a plausible sounding claim must be settled by reading the exact data point rather than by the look of the lines.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what feature best groups several curves that rise and fall through observation and reasoning, and determine that the timing of each peak, not the yearly total, sorts them, so places whose values peak in the same month belong together while the place with the largest total need not join them. They will explain that one well chosen month can make the split obvious, so two places can fall in different groups even when their totals are close.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to state that an infographic presents data using pictures, colour and layout for quick reading, and that its key or scale must be read before drawing a conclusion. They will extract stated values from a given infographic and separate what it shows from what it only suggests.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what a shaded map with a signed scale is encoding through observation and reasoning, and determine that a value from minus 100 to plus 100 marks a difference with a meaningful zero in the middle, so plus 100 means the strongest preference for one item rather than the total absence of the other. They will explain that a value near zero means a balanced difference and that the colour carries both the sign for direction and the size for strength.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what two readings a coloured time strip offers through observation and reasoning, and determine that the number of boxes a block fills gives how long an activity lasted while the position of the boxes gives when it happened, reading a clock time from the position given two boxes per hour. They will explain that a block of colour carries both duration and timing, so equal length blocks at different positions mean different times of day.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer how the choice of axis scale changes what a line graph shows through observation and reasoning, and determine that a scale fitted to the data reveals the trend while a scale too wide flattens it and one too narrow clips the values, and that the connecting segments let you read between the plotted points. They will explain that the scale is a choice that can clarify or distort, and a between point reading only estimates a value the graph does not list.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Examine the worked examples of choosing a scale, and reading between points, across different cases.

objectives.strand_name: Visualising and Interpreting Data
objectives.objective_text: Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving choosing a scale, and reading between points, across different cases.

how_to_use.intro: Each topic pairs a short, plain explanation with one interactive tool, and the whole chapter is learned by doing: predicting first, then letting the tool confirm the discovery.

points.text: Every idea is explored by hand before it is practised, and the tool only confirms a guess the student has already committed.
points.title: One tool per section

points.text: Worked examples are demonstrated in Learn mode, then the same skill is practised in Play mode where answers turn green or red.
points.title: Learn then Play

points.text: After the tool-answered practice, four reasoning items ask the learner to apply, work backwards, explain, and catch a deliberate mistake.
points.title: Think it through

points.text: A few sections carry a short video for motivation, a real-data story, or a recap; it always plays after the tool, never before, so it never pre-empts the student's own discovery.
points.title: Video after the tool

summary_stats.counts_note: One distinct tool per concept; each tool runs four mods (AI demo, Learn, Practice, Free Play), with one objective each for AI demo, Learn and Practice and none for Free Play.
summary_stats.videos_note: One 30 to 40 second curiosity hook video per topic, plus a chapter intro video and a chapter summary video of 1 to 2 minutes each.
summary_stats.tool_needed_note: Per-item boolean for how the ANSWER is entered, NOT whether to show the tool. The frontend ALWAYS renders the tool. true = the answer must be produced through the tool. false = the student reasons it out (typed/spoken) and the tool stays on screen as an aid.
summary_stats.solved_examples_note: Each solved example carries a first-person 'reasoning' field that generalises the method.
summary_stats.practice_problems_note: 244 practice items in all = (16 microconcepts x 10 tool-answered) + (16 x 4 reasoning items) + 4 proof items on the concepts that state a general claim.
summary_stats.question_repository_note: Worked-example and practice questions are no longer inline. Each learn/practice concept carries a question_bank_ref into question_repository.json; the teacher agent pulls questions from the repository at teach time. The teaching (AI-demo) concept keeps its inline source_ai_reasoning block.

authoring_rules.nesting: Each objective contains exactly one concept; each concept contains its solved examples then its practice questions.
authoring_rules.solved_examples: At least 10 per microconcept; each is demonstrated on that section's tool with numbered steps, a final answer and first-person reasoning that models how to think, not just which buttons to press.
authoring_rules.practice_questions: At least 10 tool-answered items per microconcept (marked right/wrong on the tool), followed by exactly 4 reasoning items: application, reverse, explain, error_spotting. A concept that states a general claim carries a 5th reasoning item, proof, between explain and error_spotting.

mods.does: The AI teaches the whole concept and works the higher-order reasoning questions (application, reverse, explain, error-spotting) with full step-by-step explanations, with the tool on screen; the student only watches.
The AI demonstrates the worked examples one step at a time on the tool.
The student answers the tool-answered practice questions that reinforce the worked examples.
The student freely solves any question of the same kind on the tool, neither taught nor scored.

tool_mods_legend.note: Every tool runs four mods. Teach mods are AI operated; practice and play are student operated.
